In view of the ever-increasing number of deaths resulting from marine accidents on Canada's Pacific coast, and in the light of testimony given yesterday in Vancouver before the Dubin royal commission, to the effect that there are no float-equipped rescue aircraft operating on the west coast, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Whereas the total number of Indians, Inuit and Metis in Canada is more than 1 million persons- more than the population of several of the provinces-and whereas these aboriginal peoples of Canada were never consulted with respect to the present Constitution, or agreed to its terms, nor with respect to the many federal and provincial laws which have critically affected their lives, lands and communities, and whereas the aboriginal peoples of Canada never voluntarily relinquished their political sovereignty over many areas of Canadian territory, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I, too, rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
Canadians were shocked last week when the CRTC, a federal regulatory agency, threatened to cite an individual for contempt of court because it did not approve of comments made in an intervention before the commission. That this House, being disturbed by recent actions of the CRTC which threaten the freedom of speech of individuals before the commission, calls upon the Minister of Justice to make a full investigation of this incident and report to the House on what measures he feels are necessary to ensure that federal regulatory agencies do not place themselves beyond public criticism.

subsubtopic: ROLE OF CABLE TV-PARLIAMENTARY TASK FORCE STUDY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that Canada's major cable TV operator, Mr. Ted Rogers, in a submission before the CRTC in Vancouver, proposed to "redefine the role of cable TV as a communications medium and to offer a broad range of non-broadcast interactive services"-in short, to become another common carrier-and since both the Telecommunications Carriers Association and the Telecommunications Workers Union have expressed concern that cable's intention to duplicate existing and future natural carrier functions will, among other considerations, require a vast outlay of funds for hardware to be shouldered by the consuming public, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell):
That this House accept the recommendation of both the Telecommunications Carriers Association and the Telecommunications Workers Union to establish immediately a parliamentary task force to study the economic impact of these new services contemplated by the cable industry's apparent interest in becoming a common carrier.

subsubtopic: SUBSIDIZATION OF INSULATION FOR PRE-1976 HOMES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I, too, rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under Standing Order 43. In the Speech from the Throne, the government promised to bring in an extended home insulation program. The heating season is now over, and now is an ideal time for people to work on insulating their homes so that they will be ready for next winter. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone):
That this House does hereby direct the government to forthwith introduce rules and regulations for a new Canadian Home Insulation Program to subsidize home insulation for all homes built prior to 1976, particularly homes where it is impossible for the home owner who is forced to use home heating oil and where it is impossible or next to impossible for that home owner to convert to an alternate source of energy.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: MEETING SCHEDULED FOR JUNE 9-INVITATIONS TO ATTEND- AGENDA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister relating to the constitutional meeting scheduled for June 9.
Can the Prime Minister tell the House of Commons whether a formal invitation will be issued to the Executive Council of the Yukon and the Executive Committee of the Northwest Territories to attend the June 9 constitutional meeting and to participate in those talks which might follow that meeting?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: MEETING SCHEDULED FOR JUNE 9-INVITATIONS TO ATTEND- AGENDA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the meeting of June 9 as discussed between the premiers and myself is for the premiers and the Prime Minister of Canada only. However, the Leader of the Opposition will recall that at the last constitutional conference that was convened in February, 1979, we put that item on the agenda and consulted the provinces on the possibility and the desirability, from our point of view, of involving native peoples on the one hand and making sure that their representations were made.
In so far as the Yukon and the Territories are concerned, we have always followed the practice of ensuring their presence either as observers or, in some cases, as members of the federal delegation.

subsubtopic: MEETING SCHEDULED FOR JUNE 9-INVITATIONS TO ATTEND- AGENDA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister will know that there is widespread dissatisfaction in the north at the prospect of being either excluded from a conference of heads of government or being represented there by, in effect, federal bureaucrats. The Prime Minister indicated that it is the intention of his government to urge the participation of the territories' representatives in the process, if I correctly understood him.
May I ask the Prime Minister whether it is his intention to request of the provinces that an invitation to subsequent meetings be extended to elected representatives of the people
of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, elected members of their respective councils?

subsubtopic: MEETING SCHEDULED FOR JUNE 9-INVITATIONS TO ATTEND- AGENDA
speechtext:
No, Madam Speaker. I do not want there to be any misunderstanding on this. In the past, I have encouraged the Yukon and the Northwest Territories to be present either as special observers or as members of the federal delegation. I do not intend to urge the provinces to change the practice.
At the meetings which have been held thus far under my government and all previous governments, the practice has been that federal-provincial conferences are attended by first ministers of the provinces and of the federal government, not by representatives of the Territories.

subsubtopic: MEETING SCHEDULED FOR JUNE 9-INVITATIONS TO ATTEND- AGENDA
speechtext:
The other day, in the House, the Prime Minister declined to indicate the agenda the federal government would be setting forth for the June 9 meeting because he had not received a reply from the government of Quebec.
Now that he has received a reply, would the Prime Minister tell us what agenda the government proposes for the meeting on June 9, and whether it will include a discussion of the means by which citizens of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories will be represented by people they elected, at subsequent constitutional meetings?

subsubtopic: MEETING SCHEDULED FOR JUNE 9-INVITATIONS TO ATTEND- AGENDA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, no formal agenda has been agreed to by the provinces and the federal government; nor, I believe, was it the intention to have a specific and formal agenda. The meeting is an informal one on constitutional matters generally. We, for our part, have indicated, in correspondence which I will be pleased to table later today, that we hope at these meetings to agree on at least two things: the basic principles [DOT] which must underlie our federation and, second, the method by which progress could be made in updating and modernizing the Constitution.
As to the second part of the question, that subject is not specifically on the agenda. Of course, if the matter arises on provincial initiative, or if I see fit to discuss it, I will, but I want to tell the prime minister-

A supplementary to the Prime Minister regarding the June 9 meeting. In view of the great interest in the constitutional discussion across the country, has he made a firm decision as to whether those meetings shall be held in public or in camera?
May 29, 1980

subsubtopic: MEETING SCHEDULED FOR JUNE 9-INVITATIONS TO ATTEND- AGENDA
speechtext: It was the generally expressed desire that the meeting of first ministers be private, but I believe it has already been indicated by one first minister that he intends to report everything that takes place. subsubtopic: MEETING SCHEDULED FOR JUNE 9-INVITATIONS TO ATTEND- AGENDA
speechtext: Is it the right hon. gentleman's intention, at the meetings on June 9, to explore with the premiers the possibility of establishing a regular schedule of constitutional meetings with participation not only by the federal government and the provincial governments, but also exploring the possibility of future meetings on a regular basis to include Canadians in a broader pattern than is represented at a federal-provincial conference?

subsubtopic: MEETING SCHEDULED FOR JUNE 9-INVITATIONS TO ATTEND- AGENDA
speechtext: I feel that is a very constructive suggestion and I am quite certain the discussions will take that suggestion into account. When I say we shall be looking at the process for improving our basic constitution, that should be one of the methods we would look at. But I cannot at this time say what conclusions will be reached at the meeting of first ministers.

subsubtopic: MEETING SCHEDULED FOR JUNE 9-INVITATIONS TO ATTEND- AGENDA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the letters the Prime Minister is tabling at three o'clock, one common letter to the premiers of the predominantly Englishspeaking provinces and the other to the premier of the province of Quebec, there is a language difference: I do not want to suggest there is any difference in ideas; I just want clarification in light of what the Prime Minister has just said to the House.
In the letter to the premier of the province of Quebec, the Prime Minister indicates that the subject would be to reach agreement "both on the principles and on the process of constitutional change", whereas in the letter to the other premiers, the Prime Minister simply says that the purpose of the meeting is "to lay our future plans".
Does the Prime Minister really make any distinction between those two letters and, more specifically, is it clearly his intention not to attempt to reach an agreement on any matters of substance at the June 9 meeting?

subsubtopic: MEETING SCHEDULED FOR JUNE 9-INVITATIONS TO ATTEND- AGENDA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to assure the leader of the New Democratic Party that both letters convey the same meaning and there was no intention, in the translation, of changing the emphasis of one aspect or another of the letter.
As for the second part of the question, I would ask the hon. member to repeat it.

subsubtopic: MEETING SCHEDULED FOR JUNE 9-INVITATIONS TO ATTEND- AGENDA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will include that second part in my second question. I asked the Prime Minister to indicate clearly, or reaffirm that it was not his intention to reach an agreement at the June 9 meeting, since it is private
Oral Questions
and since it is restricted to the first ministers, on any matter of substance in terms of constitutional change.
My second question, if the Prime Minister will deal with it at the same time, is this: last week he indicated an agreement in principle to the idea of including, as part of the federal delegation, leaders of opposition parties as well as, perhaps, other members of opposition parties in an attempt to get a broad, consensus approach to this serious question of constitutional change. Does he still stand by that, and is he urging his colleagues at the provincial level to establish the same principle?

subsubtopic: MEETING SCHEDULED FOR JUNE 9-INVITATIONS TO ATTEND- AGENDA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if hon. leaders of the opposition parties are willing and available, it would be my intention to meet with them next week, at their convenience, to have a discussion among ourselves to see in what direction they would hope the federal government or myself would be leading the conversations at the meeting on the ninth.
I would not expect to extract any form of binding agreement but 1 would be interested in knowing if, among ourselves, the parties represented in this House of Commons, there is some basic agreement on the general principles underlying our federalism and, indeed, the ways in which they think progress could be made in a rapid way in renewing our federalism. I am convinced that I will be enlightened by such meetings and I hope I would be able to guide my own participation on the ninth on those discussions.
In so far as the end of the previous question regarding substance is concerned, Madam Speaker, we hope that basic principles of federalism will be discussed and to that degree there will, of course, be discussions of substance. I would not expect, even in my wildest dreams, that there would be agreement on some form of words to be put in which ultimately would be an amendment to our present Constitution. If that should happen, and if 1 I of us should reach agreement at that meeting on part or the whole of a new Constitution, 1 would grab it and run.

subsubtopic: MEETING SCHEDULED FOR JUNE 9-INVITATIONS TO ATTEND- AGENDA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a final, two-part question on this important subject matter. I think the Prime Minister misunderstood the second part of my last question. I asked, does the Prime Minister agree in principle that as part of the delegation which he would lead to such a first ministers' conference on June 9, and it would not therefore be a first ministers' conference exclusively, the Canadian government delegation would include the Leader of the Opposition, myself and possibly other members of opposition parties? I would like him to answer that question.
The second part to the question, to go back to the question of representation by the Yukon and the Northwest Territories and native peoples' groups, would he agree that at subsequent meetings which take place concerning constitutional change there should be an expanded delegation coming from the federal government and the provinces, native peoples, representatives of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon who ought to have an opportunity publicly to make submissions to such meetings.

subsubtopic: MEETING SCHEDULED FOR JUNE 9-INVITATIONS TO ATTEND- AGENDA
speechtext:
In answer to the first part of the question, Madam Speaker, i believe I already gave the answer a couple of weeks ago, but I will certainly repeat it: that if a measure of agreement can emerge among ourselves as to how best we can renew federalism, and do that with considerable speed, 1 would be most happy.
I can say in advance that, if such is the case, of course I would be happy to include members of the opposition and, certainly, leaders of the opposition parties in the federal delegation. But, of course, I cannot prejudge that until we have had some discussions.
With regard to the second part of the question, my answer is that just a few weeks ago 1 met the native chiefs and elders and their political leaders in Ottawa. I gave them an assurance that any constitutional discussions which would involve subjects close to their concerns-such as aboriginal rights, local government, and so on-would be subjects on which they would be consulted, without any decision being made before we had such consultations.
I fail to see at this moment that until we in the House, and perhaps we in the House with the Indians, natives and Inuit and we in the House with the people of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, have reached some measure of agreement, it would be productive to have federal-provincial conferences at which everyone airs their point of view but no progress is made. 1 think the House is seized of the importance of making progress quickly on this matter, otherwise we would be justifiably accused of not keeping our promise to renew federalism with as much haste as possible, and I want to create conditions where we can make progress.

The point raised by my colleague, the hon. member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight), when he cited an order in council was that an order in council vesting ministerial responsibility does not vest the responsibility for reporting to Parliament for the Wheat Board in someone in the other place: it vests that responsibility, clearly and categorically, in the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin).

-to assist the Minister of Transport in the carrying out of the latter's responsibilities-
That is, in the carrying out of the Minister of Transport's responsibilities. It continues:
(a) in respect of the Canadian Wheat Board: and (b) as minister for the purposes of the Two-Price Wheat Act and the Western Grain Stabilization Act.
The order in council makes it abundantly clear that there is not another minister in another place upon whom this Minister of Transport can shuck off responsibility for the Canadian Wheat Board. It is his job to know what the Wheat Board is doing. It is his job to report to this House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

It is his job to take responsibility. It may well be simply a matter of opinion whether or not the minister is carrying out that job well. We think he is carrying it out abominably, Madam Speaker. I cannot remember a minister in my time in the House of Commons who has come into this House day after day less prepared than the Minister of Transport has in relation to very important questions relating to the Canadian Wheat Board. But that is a matter of opinion.

May 29, 1980
Privilege-Mr. McKnight
The question of privilege at stake here has to do with the attempt by this minister to deny, here, on the floor of the House of Commons, responsibilities which are clearly assigned to him by an order in council. subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a different and very important question of privilege dealing with the rights of all members of this House, and one that we can underscore as restricting members from their full opportunity to participate in Parliament. It deals with the fact that, for whatever the reasons, the government of the day has failed to put this Parliament into action, as demonstrated by the fact that as of this moment 13 out of 20 committees are not functioning. If we take a look at those committees, six of them have never met, and seven have met only to have their organizational meeting but have not met since.
In light of the discussion we just had on a question of privilege dealing with the Canadian Wheat Board, if we look at that particular institution it will be noted that the Canadian Wheat Board has a budget as large as the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan combined. It reports to no one except members of Parliament, and yet members of Parliament are denied the opportunity to call that agency to account. Members of Parliament are the only people who can call that agency to account.
If we look at the committees on agriculture, fisheries and forestry, health and welfare, justice and legal affairs, miscellaneous private bills, procedure and organization, and a great number of other committees, we find in fact that they have never met or they have in no way-

subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES
speechtext: Veterans Affairs.

subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES
speechtext:
The member of the New Democratic Party says that veterans affairs has not met. As hon. members know, if there is a motion in the committee and that motion is passed by the committee, it must be brought to this Parliament and debated here if there is a wish by any one member to call for it. However, we cannot call for that motion if the committee does not sit. We cannot speak in this chamber if those committees will not allow us to raise the motion with the possibility of passing it and therefore bringing it to this chamber.
Those members who have been here for some time are clearly aware of the narrow restriction of what is and what is not privilege: it is whether or not we are restricted to function in Parliament in this chamber. However, when we look at the issues that we could potentially face, the committee function, surely we have to come to the conclusion that you can bar a member in a committee by somehow not allowing him to speak, putting him out of the committee or physically or psychologically cutting him off. Surely you can do the same thing by never having the committees function, and thereby denying a member that right.
If you take the committee function which would bring to this Parliament a variation of activities, amendments, motions or whatever, and make it so it cannot be proceeded with here, then surely it has to be a concern when we say our right to speak or to influence this Parliament has been denied.
I wish to refer to citation 578 of Beauchesne which deals with the need to call committees early. It is citation 579(2), which puts a responsibility for that clearly on the government whip, and citation 570 which stresses that committees must give preference to due and sufficient consideration.
I am not sure what the members on the government side would consider due consideration, but today is the forty-fifth day after this Parliament resumed on April 14. Surely we do not need to wait beyond some 45-day period with more than 50 per cent of the committees either not formed or never having met for the first meeting. There are, before us, all the estimates. We should have a right to call those estimates, as members of parliament, in order to review them, analyse them, criticize them or make amendments. We should have the right to make a motion which would bring a debate to the floor of this chamber. However, we are denied that opportunity because the government of the day simply will not strike the committees or have the committees called to meet.
One of the questions that members of Parliament are starting to ask is, "Why are we here?" There are systems set up whereby we can function, work and represent our constituencies on the issues of the country. However, if they will not put the systems in place, then by default what the government is doing is making it so that Parliament will not, and cannot, work.
We see situations like the explosion of Mount St. Helens, in Washington, which is having an effect on the spawning of salmon on the west coast; but there is no fisheries and forestry committee. Very early in the spring and summer of 1980 we have had by far the largest number of acres of forest destroyed by fire that we have had in our history; but find there is no forestry committee meeting. When we find there is no forestry committee meeting, then surely the rights of members are, in fact, being denied.
I would like to quote just one other instance of this, Madam Speaker. I refer to the occasion just a few weeks ago when the member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) rose under the provisions of Standing Order 26. You will recall he was
May 29, 1980

endeavouring to bring to Your Honour's attention, and to the attention of the House, his concern about the very severe drought in the three prairie provinces. At that time, Madam Speaker, you denied the emergency debate on the following grounds-and I quote your words:
In this instance I am sure the hon. member knows that the matter can be raised in the committee where the estimates of the Department of Agriculture are currently being studied.
Madam Speaker, that was some weeks ago, yet the Standing Committee on Agriculture is only today meeting for the first time. So up to this moment, 45 days after April 14, when there was an urgent request made by one member followed by the suggestion that he could take the matter up before a committee, there has been no committee. So I would again say I think we are being denied.
If we take a look at the miscellaneous estimates committee we find that the committee met, mapped out two weeks of work, and has not met since. I think that speaks for itself about the kind and quality of work the government is directing us to do and about our inability to function. I argue that the right of members of Parliament to scrutinize estimates, to examine government policy, to analyse and make suggestions about alternative policy, belongs to every member of this House. A member is denied the privilege of being able to participate if the system denies him the opportunity to do so.
I believe I do have a question of privilege under the provisions of Standing Order 75(2), and I glean some information from that Standing Order although there are many others which are relevant. It says:
All amendments made in committee shall be reported to the House.
How can I, as a member of Parliament, affect in this House something that would come out of an extension of the House if that extension does not exist? The committees have always been viewed by members of Parliament as an extension of Parliament. When we sit in committee we are sitting in an extension of Parliament. I am sure members of all parties, when their constituents come to sit in the galleries in the afternoons and ask "Where are you?", tell them: "I am in committee, which is an extension of the House." That is a part of the House activities. Standing Order 75(2) states that all amendments adopted in committees must be brought to the House. But we cannot do this when more than half of the committees, 45 days after this Parliament met, are not sitting.
Madam Speaker, if in your judgment I have a bona fide question of privilege, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen):
That the unacceptable failure of the leader of the government in the House of Commons to give instructions or references so as to cause the committees of this House to function, be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
As a footnote, I would like to add that this is one of the committees which, by chance, happens to be meeting.

subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Yes, Madam Speaker. I would like to emphasize the remarks made by my colleague from Crowfoot (Mr. Malone), because it is absolute-
Privilege-Mr. Malone
ly unacceptable in my view that at this point in time, in the sixth week of this Parliament, a number of our committees are defective. I remember very well that when we were in committee to discuss the current rules of procedure, we ensured that it would not be necessary to wait for motions of reference from the government before estimates could be sent to a committee. In fact, once the estimates are introduced, they are automatically referred, and committees are in place because the first motions are for the nominations committee, and committees are appointed in a matter of days. But this is ended for the major part, and the government whip is directly responsible for this.
The only way we can act is to submit our grievance to the Chair. We can voice our grievances, and how! This is a tactic worthy of Marie-Antoinette, to say in the House that you can discuss a certain matter in committee when that committee does not even exist. This is not a satisfactory way to deal with matters when there is a crisis in one region of the country. When there was a dry spell in eastern Ontario, your predecessor, Mr. Lamoureux, had agreed to an emergency debate. And now, we also have rules in this respect; there is no interference with the work of the House since these emergency debates are held after the ordinary time for adjournment, such as Wednesday night. Therefore, why say that when it does not exist? However, tomorrow will be an opposition day. Such days are provided so that the opposition will use information to judge the administration of one department after having studied certain votes. But how is it possible to do that if half the committees do not meet? We cannot study the votes if we do not have them before us.
The opposition is completely frustrated in its efforts. It may be that government members do not know that we can be frustrated with respect to matters we want to raise during opposition days. And to state merely that those days exist and you may air your complaints, if it is not possible to seek out these complaints or to expound on them, this is another method worthy of Marie-Antoinette. I simply say that I agree very strongly with my colleague from Crowfoot and it is now imperative that the government whip be asked to appear before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections to explain why he has neglected his duties, and on this point I support the motion.

subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in speaking to the question of privilege raised by my friend the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone). 1, too, would like to reflect on the frustration I feel as a member of this House, duly elected and fully equal to all other members, to engage in the full parliamentary process in accordance with parliamentary traditions, and long-established and respected routines.
Without meaning any disrespect to the Chair, I think it is Your Honour's responsibility to recognize that there is an arrogance on the part of the government, a lack of co-opera-

May 29, 1980
Privilege-Mr. Malone
tion which ought to be unacceptable to the Canadian people and which is certainly unacceptable to members on this side of the House. In light of my interest in fisheries in particular, I find absolute frustration in the fact that some $300 million worth of spending under the jurisdiction of the minister responsible for fisheries is contained within the estimates for the current year, yet we in this House through the process of committee work are not able to examine those estimates. We have long, unresolved questions relating to federal fisheries licensing policy, questions related to reports which the committee should have been dealing with a year ago, and we are not even able to secure enough of the time of the House to get detailed answers from the minister responsible. It is, therefore, a travesty that the committee has not been organized, let alone called to this date after almost seven weeks of sitting of this House.
There have been two motions under Standing Order 43, one last Thursday and another again yesterday, moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnaty-shyn) censuring the government and directing it to get on with the calling of committees so that this important work might commence.
We recently had a volcanic eruption that has decimated the salmon stocks of the western Washington coastal region, and we have Washington fishermen now suggesting that they should have a greater share of the salmon yield from the Fraser River. That is a matter of some urgency in which all of our west coast fishermen have considerable interest. We should be able to question the minister on what approaches he is making to his American counterpart, and what initiatives he is taking on behalf of west coast fishermen to see that their interests are protected.
Of course, as my colleague the hon. member for Crowfoot mentioned, and other colleagues might wish to go into greater detail, we have forest fires raging across this country, a matter which ought to be before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.
The fishing season is under way, yet the minister has yet to make any announcement on fishing licensing regulations and fee structures in the commercial fishery and the sport fishery. There are fishermen who are expecting to go out fishing or, indeed, are out already who do not know what size salmon they should be throwing back into the water. There is a whole host of related questions that we know the minister has under deliberation.
In the Speech from the Throne we heard reference to a special landing tax or levy against the catch of west coast fishermen, and we want to question the minister about that concept because we think the fishermen of Canada are very, very concerned about what that will mean to their incomes this year, particularly given a very tight situation in terms of the prices that world markets are yielding.
There are important conservation considerations, the east and west coast joint Canada-U.S. negotiations affecting our
fisheries, and there was a review of the Fresh Water Fish Marketing Corporation in process, all questions that have gone without answers because the government opposite is frustrating the process of this Parliament and its opportunity to get detailed answers to these questions.
In supporting this question of privilege I would urge that you, Madam Speaker, consider very seriously that the work of Parliament is being frustrated. Ministers are abdicating their obligations to members of Parliament and this is a mark of their arrogance and their lack of respect for Parliament. I think this is absolutely inexcusable.

subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will be rising, I hope, later today on another matter of privilege, or a point of order, I suppose, technically, but that matter pales by comparison with the import of the motion that my colleague, the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone), has put forward this afternoon having to do with the failure of some of our standing committees of Parliament to meet. While 1 had not intended to speak on the motion, I was so moved by his eloquence and the eloquence of other members I felt obliged to respond. The motion relates fundamentally to the rights of every member of this House, regardless of party and regardless of where any particular member might sit.
The hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon) has referred to the failure of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry to meet, a failure even to have an organizational meeting. He has discussed some important and urgent matters relating to fisheries. For just a moment or two I would like to elaborate on that point by illustrating the importance of some other issues coming under the rubric of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.
I refer in particular to the urgent issues having to do with the environment, in respect of which I am the official spokesman of the Progressive Conservative Party. All of the urgent problems to which I might refer could not be itemized in the short time I have at my disposal. But I should mention, and it is only an illustration, the problem of acid rain, a form of pollution that is devastating our forests, our waters, our air, our land and our wildlife; indeed, it is threatening human life itself. That is a matter which could be dealt with effectively, not just in Parliament on the floor of the House of Commons itself, but as well in the forum that standing committees provide.
Another example is resource development. Huge initiatives being taken-for instance, in the Arctic-threaten our environment, our precious and delicate ecosystems there. That is an issue, too, that should be dealt with in the relevant standing committees of the House which are failing to meet.
What about the proposals for tanker routes down our coasts and the threat they pose to our environment? And what about oil exploration everywhere, including that in my own region of Atlantic Canada and the threat it presents to our fish stocks? Another illustration is agricultural spraying. All such matters cry out for urgent attention by every member of this House regardless of party and regardless of where a member might
May 29, 1980

sit. Because these standing committees are not meeting, the government is, in effect, failing to provide members of the House of Commons with one of the most important forums in which to address national problems. Members of Parliament are, consequently, being denied a fundamental right.
All those issues I mentioned, and many others that could be referred to, need to be discussed in standing committees. Since they are not, we are being denied the right, for example, to hold relevant ministers accountable for their portfolios. It is a basic principle of parliamentary democracy and of responsible government that ministers must account to members of the House of Commons in every parliamentary forum, whether in the House of Commons or in standing committees, which are, as one member pointed out, an extension of this House. We do not have that opportunity, for some of the standing committees have yet to meet. We are, therefore, being denied our full privileges, and in the process the principle of responsible government itself is being undermined.
It is for those reasons, and for many others, that I take great pride in supporting the motion put forward by the hon. member for Crowfoot, and I urge all other members to support it likewise.

subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in my view there is no more fundamental question of privilege raised in this House than this; that has been my experience after serving eight years in this House. It is further testimony, to my way of thinking, to the arrogance of this particular government in denying the right of members on all sides of the House to exercise their functions; hence privilege. This is the definition of privilege. Members are being denied the possibility of even exercising their full functions to legislate, to inquire and to hold ministers to account for the performance of their duties.
There was a package of parliamentary reform available for presentation by the government in the Thirty-first Parliament. It was to have been placed before the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization and it would have obviated this particular problem we are now facing. That package would have permitted, had it been accepted, the members of the committees to call the committees together without having to wait on an inefficient, ineffective and arrogant government to agree, to condescend to allow committees to be brought together in order to fulfil their functions, or one of the functions of Parliament, and to permit members of this Parliament to perform their functions.
That package would have been brought before the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization in this Parliament had the committee been allowed to be brought together by an order of the House. There should be an automatic reference of every ministerial report, any departmental report, to committee so that the committee would have, by virtue of the tabling of that particular report, access to the minister in charge of the department.
Privilege-Mr. Malone
My colleagues have spoken of the various problems this country is facing owing to the drought, forest fires, the fall-out from Mount St. Helens and its effects on the forestry industry, the fishing industry and agriculture. But there is no possibility of discussing these subjects in committee because under the standing rules it is the government alone that makes the reference to the House. The House concurs in the reference once the government has drawn it up, but there has to be, if this Parliament is to have any meaning whatever and if your role, Madam Speaker, is to have any meaning whatever, with all due respect, a means for this Parliament to function and for members to exercise the duties and resDonsibilities for which they were sent to this Parliament by their constituents.
Therefore, I support every single word, comma, apostrophe and parenthesis, the whole statement, of my colleague, the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone). I encourage you, Madam Speaker, to rule that we should have the means now of calling the committees together so that we may fulfil our duties.

subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, I was just saying that intelligent reading of our Standing Orders shows that Standing Order 65(1) stipulates as follows:
At the commencement of the first session of each Parliament, a striking committee, consisting of seven members, shall be appointed, whose duty it shall be to prepare and report, within the first ten sitting days after its appointment, lists of members to compose the following standing committees of the House:
Then, a list is given of 20 standing committees of the House. We have fulfilled our obligation, Madam Speaker. The striking committee was appointed and the list drawn up of hon. members chosen to sit on those committees. The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) brought up two points which deserve consideration. The first concerns the organization of those committees, and the second the fact that some committees, though constituted, are not sitting.
On the first point, 1 want to advise the hon. member that I am surprised by his statement because, according to my information, the overwhelming majority of the standing committees of the House have been organized. In fact, it seems

speakeroldname: Hon. Janies A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, would the hon. minister permit a question? I am not quarrelling with what the minister had to say, with one notable exception. My question is simply this: Does he take the position that only the government has the right to call an organizational meeting of a committee, just as only the government has the right to set the day when Parliament will meet? Parliament cannot meet itself because it does not have a Speaker; only the government can set that date. By the same token, only the government can decide when a committee will meet after it has been struck. Is the minister taking the position in this House that the government does not have the responsibility to convene a meeting of a committee after it has been struck for the purposes of that committee organizing itself and electing a chairman and a vice-chairman?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES
speechtext:
I indicated clearly a few minutes ago, at least I thought it was clear, that some hon. members have maintained that committees which were organized had not met and I said they had not given any proof to their arguments demonstrating that the government was to blame if some committees had not yet met. I stated this clearly.
In answer to my colleague who asked whether it is up to the government to see that these committees organize themselves, in my view the government must surely have an important role to play in this respect. For my part, when there is a problem I have always been ready to discuss it with the parliamentary leaders of the other parties in order that all House services work as smoothly as possible. I have great respect for the rights and privileges of the opposition as well as ours and I like to see the opposition participate. And if there had been serious reasons, serious complaints or consequences for the opposition stemming from the fact that some committees, albeit a small number of them, had not yet been organized it seems to me that I would have heard about it from my eminent colleagues who are parliamentary leaders of the official opposition and of the NDP, but I have never heard a complaint of this nature.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the minister. The advice I have been given is that the committees which have not met are the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills and Standing Orders, and the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. That is my understanding of the committees which have not met. Some of them are quite important with respect to issues, as members have indicated.
Now that the issue is here in the House, I have a question for the minister. Would the government House leader under-
Privilege-Mr. Malone
take to speak to the members of the committee-and I will for my part undertake to speak to members of the committee on my side of the House-so that they can be urged to ensure, in the event that it is found there is no question of privilege, that those committees get going? Although there may be no legal responsibility on the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard)-he may take that view-I think he has had the sense of the House. 1 now speak to him in his capacity as House leader. Having had the sense of the House, will he take some initiatives to get those committees going?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, this is what I referred to earlier in my remarks. Considering on the one hand that almost three-quarters of an hour were lost arguing about a question of privilege, which it is not, and on the other hand that this is the first time I have heard any complaints about this, I offered my services to speed up the organizing process of those committees that are not yet organized and to check whether there are serious or valid reasons why the organized committees have not yet met. Therefore I would repeat the offer I was pleased to extend to my colleague, the Leader of the Official Opposition, and I extend the same offer to the Leader of the New Democratic Party, who seems to be in agreement.

subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES

Would the House leader accept that form of a reference? He said that it is not the government's responsibility to produce references. If we can produce references in that way, I would be delighted to learn of it, because it will happen tomorrow.

Madam Speaker, to answer the question, first there is nothing to hinder the hon. member from introducing a motion under Standing Order 43. Of course, we decide whether it is truly urgent, as we did on all those that came up until now. I cannot guarantee that the 281 members in this House will agree to a motion by the hon. member to refer any subject to a committee. Second, we jealously maintain nonetheless the government's prerogative under Standing Order 18(2), and we are responsible for establishing the order of things here. What I said earlier, and I would have expected my learned colleague to grasp it immediately, is that we sometimes refrain from referring subjects without consulting with opposition members.

May 29, 1980
Privilege-Mr. Malone
When I said that Parliament was involved, opposition members were involved in the references, I made it very clear later that this usually follows a lack of agreement in a debate that the subject or legislation or motion be referred to committee, whence the contribution by members from both sides of the House, including the hon. member who just put the question.

subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES

Should such a motion be put tomorrow, as indeed it was yesterday by the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn), would the House leader give us his assurance that he would urge all members of the government caucus to support such a motion? Would he make that commitment today and show leadership to this House, in view of the recognition he has given of the fact that he believes along with us that it is time we got on with meeting in committee?

subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am afraid my hon. colleague misunderstood my remarks. 1 encourage him-I do not wish to disappoint him-to read my answers. I think they completely cover the subject. I recognized no responsibility, all I offered was my co-operation. I therefore submit this is no valid question of privilege. We are ready to co-operate and we never had any complaints before today. For the rest, 1 would encourage him to read my remarks and he will see and understand my position.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. MALONE-FAILURE TO CONVENE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES
speechtext:
It seems to me that in the question of privilege which has been raised, there are two main issues which I must deal with. First, that the committees have not met. The arguments and suggestions which have been presented have led me to believe that committees have been set up, but the main grievance seems to stem from the fact that some of them have not met. The other question on which it would seem I am expected to rule has to do with an urgent issue which hon. members feel they could not debate. They suggest that this is an important issue and that the House should deal with it forthwith. As to the setting up of committees, this clearly comes under the organization of the business of the House and as a rule, as indicated by an hon. member, it normally depends on the initiative of the whip, as expressed in Beauchesne's citation No. 579. But it is not up to me to weigh the reasons why committees are meeting or not meeting. This is completely beyond the responsibility of the Chair. I am not certain, but 1 think that there were assurances that some committees would meet so that the question which some members consider urgent could be debated.
As I was given notice of this question of privilege, I noted that the Standing Committee on Agriculture, which is mentioned in the question of privilege, was meeting this afternoon at 3.30 and that the minister would be present at the meeting. Of course, the committee is now considering the estimates.
Some will say that this urgent question is not on the order of the committee, but members could try to raise it anyway and they might obtain satisfaction.
In any case, it seems to me that I must also consider the urgency of the question raised, because some time ago, concerning a motion moved under the provisions of Standing Order 26, I gave a decision which said in essence that other procedures could be used to debate the matter, including the fact that certain committees were to meet at a later date which I was unable to specify. These other procedures would, of course, be questions during question period, motions moved by hon. members and opposition days. In fact, what I want to emphasize, in accordance with my earlier decision on the above mentioned motion, is that there are procedures which can be used to debate these urgent matters.
However, in view of the importance of the question raised, in view of the dissatisfaction of some members concerning committee meetings which are not held, and in view of the fact that the question, as presented by some members, exceeds the limits of what could be discussed in the Standing Committee on Agriculture-I believe that certain members raised the issues of the environment and fisheries, and I do not know now whether these committees have been able to meet yet or not- in view of this situation and the importance of this issue, I would like, if I may, to review all the documents and see whether there will be other opportunities to discuss this question in the House, and I shall therefore defer my decision on this motion.

subtopic: MR. ROCHE  CONSTITUENTS REFUSED ACCESS BY SECURITY STAFF TO MEMBER'S OFFICE
MR. ROCHE  CONSTITUENTS REFUSED ACCESS BY SECURITY STAFF TO MEMBER'S OFFICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am rising on a question of privilege at this, my first opportunity to do so, on a matter that affects the rights of all members and certainly affects my rights as a member.
At 1.40 p.m. today five constituents of mine, whose visit was anticipated by me and who were introduced at the front desk of this building where I maintain my own office, were not allowed past the front desk and were, in effect, barred from going to my office, despite the fact that they were, as I say, properly introduced. Moreover, one of my secretaries was sent to the front desk to personally escort these people to my office.
I feel that this is an interference with my right to receive constituents in my office. I am conscious of the security problems, particularly in this building. I have always notified the security officials when I am expecting a large number of constituents. Today, the arrival of the five constituents was, as I say, anticipated. They were rudely treated. My secretary who went personally to escort them was harassed. My staff is owed an apology by the security staff at the very least.
But in any event, I think there is a larger point at issue here, that irrespective of the security provisions of this building, I do
May 29, 1980

not think it is particularly helpful to members of Parliament when their own constituents who come to visit them in a properly programmed manner are treated in a way in which they are made to feel unwelcome and in which they are shaken, as indeed these people were today. I believe that it is the right of a member of Parliament to bring constituents to his office and, moreover, to bring them to the gallery which is provided for opposition members.
These people were denied access to that gallery. The ordinary procedure is for members of Parliament to issue passes. The constituents line up in turn and if there is room in that gallery then they get in. It is not the function of the security staff at the front door of this building to bar people entrance to my office where they can obtain a pass and then take their chances of getting into the gallery.
I feel that it is an important provision, Madam Speaker. I will not take up the time of the House on the matter, but I would ask, respectfully, Madam Speaker, that you investigate this incident and make sure that the security staff operates in such a way that they are protecting the building, but not turning away people who have a legitimate right of access to the members' offices.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. ROCHE  CONSTITUENTS REFUSED ACCESS BY SECURITY STAFF TO MEMBER'S OFFICE
speechtext:
Indeed, the hon. member has not raised a question of privilege but rather a matter of security which is under my responsibility. I am most surprised at the facts which the hon. member has related. I am sure that he is relating these facts correctly, but usually the staff at the front door or any of the doors of the House of Commons is most courteous.
Of course, we have given instructions with regard to security, that people should give their names and tell the security officers where they intend to go. We have juggled in our minds whether we would oblige any member of Parliament to send someone down to greet the people he is expecting, because that is the only way that we can ensure that these people do not go walking around and entering offices which they clearly did not want to visit at the time they presented themselves at the door. That is not a very difficult matter, but it could make the atmosphere a bit unfriendly if we had to resort to that kind of provision.
I am very surprised at the facts which the hon. member has presented and I will certainly inquire as to what exactly took place. Nobody should harass anybody in this House, but perhaps they had some reason for acting in the way they did. At any rate I will, of course, apologize to the hon. member's constituents, because I am sure like all of our constituents they want to be welcomed in Parliament.

subsubtopic: DREE-GRANTS TO INDUSTRIES-CONSTITUENCY OF LEEDS-GRENVILLE
speechtext:
1.	Will the government consider extending the designated DREE areas to include grants to medium and major industries in the constituency of Leeds-Grenville?
2.	For what reasons are Renfrew and Cornwall designated for grants to medium and major industries when Leeds-Grenville is not?
3.	On what date were designated DREE areas last changed or in any way modified with respect to grants to medium and large industries?
4.	Was Leeds-Grenville ever considered and, if not, for what reason?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre De Bane (Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
subsubtopic: DREE-GRANTS TO INDUSTRIES-CONSTITUENCY OF LEEDS-GRENVILLE
speechtext:
The response for the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is as follows:
1.	The constituency of Leeds-Grenville is currently eligible for assistance under the Small Business Incentives program of the Eastern Ontario Subsidiary Agreement. In view of this assistance, the need for fiscal restraint and, consequently the limited development funds available, an extension of the area designated for RDIA assistance is not anticipated at this time.
2.	Cornwall is not within the area currently designated for RDIA assistance. However, from April 1, 1971 to June 30, 1973, Stormont-including Cornwall, Glengarry and Prescott counties were designated under the RDIA as part of Region "C", comprising Montreal and surrounding regions. Part of Renfrew county (including the town of Renfrew) was designated for RDIA assistance on the basis of such factors as low population and employment growth, high unemployment and remoteness from metropolitan Toronto and other large market areas. In Leeds-Grenville and other parts of southern Ontario, more favourable economic conditions have generally prevailed.
3.	From April 8, 1970, until December 31, 1975, Renfrew-Pembroke was designated under the DREE Act as a special area, allowing industry in the area to receive similar assistance to that provided under the RDIA program. As of January 1, 1976, the RDIA designated area was expanded to include part of Renfrew county.
4.	Yes. As part of its ongoing efforts, DREE continuously monitors the economic circumstances of all regions of the province, including Leeds-Grenville. RDIA boundaries are thus reviewed, as conditions warrant, in order to ensure their continuing appropriateness.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, May 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen that Bill C-30, to provide supplementary borrowing authority for the fiscal year 1980-81, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it always gives me great pleasure to rise in my place in this House and debate the business of the House. Today I have particular pleasure in debating Bill C-30, the borrowing bill- a bill in which the government of Canada is asking for the authority to borrow $12 billion for the current year.
We have heard some eloquent debates in this House. One was a two-hour debate by the former minister of finance, "Honest John Crosbie," who put forth a most magnificant case in regard to the need to debate this bill in depth. Then we heard a dissertation from "Slippery Allan," as 1 call him, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), who spoke for a bare few minutes on a bill of great import. In watching him I was quite certain he would be a fine curler. He is an excellent sweeper, he can sure curl around a stone or an issue, and he can talk forever without saying anything.
The minister is offering this House an economic statement pointing to more of the same that has been handed out by the Liberal government during the decade of the seventies. What were the over-all economic directions of the Liberal government during the seventies? First, uncontrolled government growth, literally a form of de facto socialism. Second, a major preoccupation with the redistribution of wealth through a federal bureaucratic empire of enormous proportions. Third, the creation of debt to unload upon future generations-the creation of debt at enormous rates. Until this year, the debt creation, as far as I understand it, is in the order of $60 billion. Fourth, the promotion of consumption rather than production through every process known to governments. A vicious cycle of credit and the printing of paper money, therefore laying down the foundations of recurring inflation. Fifth, a massive subjugation economically of municipal and provincial governments to the bureaucratic direction of a centralized, political will.
It is this package of policies pushed to unreasonable levels that is tearing this nation apart. It is the federal government's unlimited and uncontrolled spending policies in provincial jurisdictions that is the primary cause of the constitutional difficulties that now exist in this country.
1 want to touch very briefly on one or two of these five policy points. Just a little over a year ago all governments in Canada spent approximately 42 per cent of the gross national product of the nation. What that means is that government at the three levels took from the people 42 cents of every dollar they earned, and they spent those dollars in accordance with their priorities.
Interestingly enough, in 1968 the provincial and municipal governments spent 46 per cent of the total spending of governments in Canada and the federal government spent 54 per cent. A decade later this was reversed and the provincial and municipal governments in Canada spent 53 per cent of total government expenditures and the federal government spent 47 per cent.
What this shows is a terrible desire by municipalities and provincial governments to control their own economic destiny. What it shows is that the federal government has been the catalyst to push growth at the provincial level and the municipal level to counteract the growth of the federal government which was running away during the seventies.
Rather interestingly, in this new Parliament what has now been given to us in the economic statement is an indication that the federal level of spending in relation to the gross national product will grow by 2 per cent in one year, from approximately 20 per cent of the gross national product to 22 per cent of the gross national product. As hon. members know, federal government expenditures are to be in the order of $60 billion in 1980. This is literally about 22 per cent of the gross national product of this nation. This is a startling 2 per cent increase in just one year.
If anyone could put any type of term to it, it is galloping socialism. This is being done through borrowings, not through the collection of taxes, because the taxes will only supply $45 billion, and somewhere between $14 billion and $15 billion will be borrowings. This is catastrophic for the long term. Who is going to pay this debt? Who is asked to pay this debt on behalf of the nation? What is tearing this country apart is the absolute concentration by the federal government on the redistribution of the wealth, potential and opportunity of this nation.
Western Canada is now looking desperately for manpower. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) went out to the west and indicated on his return here the vital need for technicians and people to go to western Canada to fuel the western Canadian economy.
May 29, 1980

Why are people not going to western Canada? Because they are being kept immobile through handouts in the rest of the nation. These handouts are primarily given by the federal government. This is an exciting nation because of size, because of potential and resources. The young people in this nation have all this potential before them, but they are not seeking opportunity in this nation where there is opportunity. I ask the question again, why are they not doing that? Has this government had the determination, the honesty and the courage to look at that very question and answer it in this House? The federal government has used its spending power to keep the young entrenched, doing nothing, being unproductive and on welfare in part of the nation where there is no opportunity.
Let me speak very briefly about the accumulation of federal debt. The federal debt has risen to dangerous proportions. It is in excess of $60 billion and is rising this year by some $14 billion. That is about $3,500 of debt per capita. It is rising at some $700 per capita per year. Indeed, approximately 15 per cent of the federal budget now services debt.
A family of four existing in this nation effectively has a debt associated with it of $15,000. A family of four has to pay the interest on the debt of this nation. It has to pay interest on a debt of $15,000 incurred by the federal government, apart from having to pay its mortgage and the interest on the mortgage. This is catastrophic.
I have not had the opportunity to review conditions in every other nation, but I can say categorically that no nation in this world, with the potential, the wealth and the resources it has, is in any type of situation that this nation is in today. There has been absolute and abject mismanagement over a decade of irresponsibility by a Liberal government that should have been dethroned long ago.

speechtext: Look who is talking.

speechtext: I have got them excited now, Mr. Speaker. I thought they were going to be silent, but it is obvious that they are alive over there.

speechtext: Because we are hearing untruths.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
One has to be appalled, and I for one am, by the irresponsibility of government during the decade of the seventies.
Borrowing Authority Act
We managed to get into government by the people rejecting the Liberal government in 1979, and we tried to deal with the economic problems of this nation honestly, forthrightly, with pragmatism, knowing that it was going to be difficult but that hard decisions had to be made. So we specifically set out to control the mounting debt of Canada as we are moving toward national bankruptcy. Second, we set out to contain the growth of the federal government and make it more effective and responsible. Third, we established a comprehensive energy policy needed to make Canada self-sufficient in oil by 1990, and establishing a sound strategy for Canadian energy selfsufficiency for the next century. Fourth, we established a small business incentive growth policy, coupled with major employment stimulation processes, particularly for young Canadians, to tide this nation through a most difficult period which we knew was coming. Some people termed it short-term pain for long-term gain. It did not help us during the election of February 18, but it was an honest approach taken with the greatest degree of courage.
I say that the type of attitude being exemplified in this House now-a week ago, a month ago-by a minister who gave an economic statement without the courage to come out with a budget at the earliest opportunity, means that there is no one who is going to bankrupt this nation faster than that government over there. I wish it would come to its senses.
1 want to be more specific on energy. Most of my life has been spent dealing with energy of one form or another-at least most of my professional life. Therefore, I feel 1 have an appreciation of some aspects of energy.
I want to talk briefly about the flow of capital from rising energy prices and the direction it would take in this nation, and I would like to indicate why it should or should not take that direction. Second, what I want to talk about rather specifically is the constitutional prerogatives of provincial resource price-setting. In 1974 I was president of the Canadian Council of Resources and Environment Ministers of Canada. At the first conference I sponsored as president, I asked for a detailed examination of the constitutional prerogatives of a province in connection with its resources; in other words, what it can do and what it cannot do, when it can do it and so forth. We produced a magnificent report which 1 would like to refer to periodically through my speech this afternoon.
First of all, I would like to speak a little bit about the supply of conventional oil in the world and the supply of conventional oil in Canada. Much of the conventional oil that exists in the world now was discovered in a different economic time-frame. It was discovered under a low-cost regime, and so we have established throughout the world a series of conventional oil reservoirs.
I have said in the past that no one knows the value of the oil in the ground in a conventional reservoir. It is one of the most valuable commodities on this earth. No one can put a price on it, a market price if you wish, or a value because it developed over billions of years. It is a hydrocarbon of enormous value, enormous ability and flexibility in terms of its use by humanity.

May 29, 1980
Borrowing Authority Act
We have now gone in the world from a position of supply and pricing to a position of conventional oil conservation. We have moved massively in that direction. They have shown wisdom in the Middle East. The prevalent wisdom of Mexico was well displayed in this House recently. They have cut exports to Canada and have not committed themselves on a long-term basis to supplying us with 100,000 barrels a day, but only 50,000. That indicates without equivocation that the conventional oil reservoirs of their nation have to be extended and the rate of production of those reservoirs has to be reduced. The value of that commodity is so great for the future that it is sheer hypocrisy, in fact almost a crime, to drain the reservoirs at the earlierst possible opportunity and at the fastest rate possible.
The same applies in Canada, particularly in Alberta. Alberta has moved from a position of price being the most important matter in connection with its conventional oil reserves, to recognizing that maintaining the capacity of its reservoirs over the longest possible period is the single most important criterion. That government has to do that because it is the will of the people of Alberta, and Alberta owns those resources.
What did Saskatchewan say? There was a most remarkable dissertation along this same line. Indeed, from here on there will be a delay in the tertiary recovery of their reservoirs and every mechanism will be used to limit production. On April 22, 1980, in the legislation of Saskatchewan, Mr. R. A. Larter asked the following question:
Mr. Speaker, a question to the minister for Kelsey-Tisdale. In light of huge natural gas discoveries in British Columbia, and in light of what Premier Lougheed stated last night on television that the quickest way to strengthen the Canadian dollar was to export massive amounts of natural gas, is the minister now prepared to accept the fact that there is a little more natural gas than what he anticipates? Are you ready now to do more exploring in Saskatchewan and prop up this concept that there is a lot of natural gas available?
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, I've indicated to the member on previous occasions that we are reviewing the policy in respect of natural gas exploration and development in the province of Saskatchewan. We do believe that we have the probability of discovering larger quantities of gas than we thought was the case 10 years ago. A lot of that assumption is based on the success that Alberta has enjoyed, and to a lesser degree, that British Columbia has enjoyed, in the last decade in proving up pools of gas. We are not so ambitious to open the gates, as I believe the member is alluding to, because of the problems which go along with that. We have Alberta in particular indicating that they have a surplus of gas for a shorter medium-term period of time, and are seeking very ambitiously, large export permits into the United States.
I would suggest to the member that if we were to expand gas exploration and development in Saskatchewan, we would not want to attain that level of shorter medium-term extra capacity. Because we would like to guarantee that the pools of gas we have in the province of Saskatchewan will guarantee and give assurance to Saskatchewan consumers in years to come, that we will not be the victims of imported gas from outside this province, and pay what may well be a very heavy penalty in order to have that source of energy available to us.
I recommend this policy to the members of this House. It is a very deliberate policy in Saskatchewan to delay exploration and development so that the reserves in Saskatchewan can be maintained for that province in future years. I could go on with this topic for some time, but I want to cover a few other areas of the energy scenario, and I know time goes by quickly.

speechtext: 1 have listened quite attentively to the hon. member for quite a while. I wonder if he is on the same bill. I draw to the attention of the hon. member that we are considering Bill C-30, known as the borrowing authority bill. I invite the hon. member to address his remarks to that bill.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
I have been advised by some members of this House that when the government brings in a bill for authority to borrow $12 billion to cover its debts in all areas, we have before this House for debate all areas of government activity where these borrowings are to be used. It is in that light that I am discussing this bill today. I can think of no more important matter than the question of energy. With regard to oil compensation, I understand this government may need in the area of $5 billion, and they will need it soon. There is no more fundamental matter than the energy question when discussing this bill.
I want to speak very briefly on distribution of the money. I had an opportunity to look at the gross dollar generation of the whole mining industry, which includes oil and gas. The generation of dollars in this nation from mining each year is in the order of $22 billion. Of that, about $12 billion is for oil and gas and $10 billion for minerals, building materials and other products in the mining area.
Where does this $12 billion go? With the price of energy now, this $12 billion floats primarily westward, but a substantial proportion comes back eastward through the federal government taxation system in the form of individual taxes, corporation taxes and so forth. The $12 billion that flows westward represents approximately 4.5 per cent of the gross national product of this nation. Of that, approximately 2 per cent comes back east to the rest of the nation. Therefore the net flow of capital westward from oil and gas, a resource owned by western Canada, is in the order of 2.5 per cent of the gross national product per year.
What Liberal government can say that is too great a flow of dollars westward, or to any other region of this nation in order to upgrade it? I would like any member of this House to tell me that is too much per year when in fact this nation has such dynamic potential.
Let me go further and refer to the speech made the other night by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). There is a great deal of foolishness in that speech. I am surprised that a minister of his calibre would make such foolish statements as he did in that speech.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Not foolish, sinister.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
He obviously had an objective. It was not putting the case for a united Canada. I quote from his speech:
If we were to go to 85 per cent of the international price tomorrow, and assuming no further international oil price increases, we would increase the revenues flowing to industry, provinces and the federal government, assuming gas prices rose in tandem with oil prices, by about $14 billion.
The $14 billion represents 4.5 per cent of the gross national product of this nation. Is that too much? Is that too high in
May 29, 1980

terms of boosting the capacity of the regions? Why do the young people of the rest of the nation not go to where there is all this opportunity? I did in 1950 when 1 graduated in Alberta. There was no opportunity there at all. There were 64 of us who graduated as chemical engineers. Sixty-two came to Ontario to find opportunity. We were mobile in this nation. It was the greatest thing 1 ever did in my life.
I spent six years in Ontario, traversed the United States and then went back west again. I made the circuit three times. It is an exhilarating experience for young people. It is a tremendously unifying force for this nation. It brings all regions together. Young people get to know this nation from one end to the other. The idea of taking 42 per cent of the wealth of this nation, and trying to distribute it from the centre to fix people where they are without opportunity is ludicrous. I have never any difficulty with equalization on a health basis and for providing assistance to senior citizens wherever they may be across the nation, but I have a great deal of difficulty with this administration from the centre trying to collect funds from all over the country to maintain the immobility of young, dramatic people who should be developing the west, the north and the eastern part of this land. That is the fundamental reason this nation is creaking and almost falling apart. That is the fundamental reason this nation is tearing itself apart-because the federal government has used its unlimited spending power to create a situation which cannot sustain itself; all it does is go into debt more every year to sustain this unnatural and insupportable economic situation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
