speechtext:
It is a crime. It is a crime against the well-being of this nation. It is a crime against Canadians. I wish they would get some good advice on the other side and recognize that while the federal government should, indeed, have umbrella powers to bind confederation, it should not get itself involved in every corner and nook of this country with its bureaucratic regime feeding dollars, and with DREE trying to prop up this situation, when people could be used in some other part of the nation.
Mr. Speaker, I shall speak briefly on the oil price scenario, but before I do so I should like to quote a couple of statements by the minister of energy, that eloquent man who feels he is an expert in the energy area. This is what he said:
Let me turn for a moment to natural gas. It too must rise, we are told, because Alberta has depleting resources and will soon run out of revenue. At the same time we are told that we should export more gas because we have growing supplies and will continue to have growing supplies for as far into the future as one would care to look.
Again, I am baffled by the logic. Should Canadians pay another $4 billion a year for natural gas even though we have a huge surplus of it and growing exports? Remember, of the $4 billion about $500 million would go to the federal government, about $1.5 billion to the Alberta government and $2 billion to the industry.
Does the federal government not realize that it collects income taxes from all the wealth which goes to pay wages in the west and brings it back here at the rate of 33 per cent or 40
Borrowing Authority Act
per cent or 25 per cent of all those wages that are paid? Do they not realize that it comes right back in this direction through equipment purchases, income tax, corporate taxes and so forth?
Then the minister says:
I think we should be honest with each other. The position of the Alberta government has nothing to do with security of supply. It wants a higher price for natural gas because it believes that it has a right to higher revenues.
Mr. Speaker, I was part of a government which set drilling incentives in Alberta. The industry was drying up. There were no federal incentives and the Alberta government ended up paying 95 per cent of the cost of every dry hole drilled in the province and beyond. It is beyond my understanding that a minister in this government could suggest in a speech that the Alberta government has had nothing to do with gas reserves in the province of Alberta. That is absolutely false.
I see my time is running out, Mr. Speaker. I still have much to say, but I will try to get through somehow. Here is a further quotation from the minister of energy:
We have two opposing political thrusts in this country: regionalism and interdependence. We understand and support the desire of people in outlying regions to gain more control over their lives. I think it is due; many would say overdue. But provinces can't afford to pursue autonomy by undermining interdependence.
Interdependence-pooling of strengths-is what makes this nation great, why the whole adds up to more than the sum of its parts-
I think I was one of the first to use that statement at a Man and Resources conference some few years ago. How can a minister make statements of the kind he did, Mr. Speaker? Regionalism and interdependence are not incompatible. They are mutually supportive in every way. Strong regions provide interdependence in this country through the equalization process, through the taxation process. How could a minister of the Crown, supposedly an intelligent minister, suggest that these two processes are incompatible? I can only think that the minister is massively confused and fails to recognize the nature of this country; he has been so blinded by the Quebec referendum. It is sad. What else does he say? I quote:
We just came out of a referendum in which we fought hard for a united Canada. We defeated those who wanted political sovereignty with economic association. We did not carry out this difficult battle to get economic sovereignty with political association.
The minister is using terms foolishly, like a fool, like an arrogant school debater trying to create discord and division. What is economic sovereignty? It is inseparable from political sovereignty. The two are literally the same thing. Economic sovereignty means the collection and levying of all taxes by the sovereign state, as Quebec indicated in its program for sovereignty-association. What else does it mean? It means the state shall set all its commodity prices, import taxes, export taxes, excise taxes and so on. It means the conduct of all national and international negotiations in connection with the pricing of commodities. It means the printing of its own money, the establishment of its own banks and its own credit. That is what economic sovereignty means. Mr. Speaker, I ask the minister to get up in an honest way and tell the members

Of course, what we want, not so much the documents themselves, is some idea of what progress we may or may not be making as a result of the studies, papers and books that are produced on various subjects with the intention of improving efficiency in the public service.
The Treasury Board secretariat has carried out cyclical audits since delegation of the authority to classify positions up to SX-2 was given to departments and agencies some six or seven years ago. Although this activity provided information about the administration of various aspects of the system, the subjective selection of positions used did not allow quantitative statements about classification for a particular department or the whole public service.
Therefore, in 1976 a project known as "Classification Evaluation" was established with three stages, and the report referred to in the motion deals with stage one, which was to develop and apply a scientific sampling scheme that would enable statements to be made with confidence about the quality of the output of the classification system.
For the survey design a sampling method was selected. The public service is divided into departments and agencies, and within each department positions are divided into occupational groups, and each group is divided into levels. The disadvantage is that proportional sampling applies the same sample ratio, in this case one out of every 69 positions, to all strata in the
May 29, 1980

population. As a result, for small departments the method generated such a small sample that it did not provide a meaningful estimate.
The sample taken outside the national capital area represented 1.5 per cent of the public service. The postal operations groups were excluded because the sample would have been dominated by those large groups. Thus the figures I mention are from some 135,000 public servants outside the national capital area.
The evaluation process consisted of a comparison of performed duties with the classification standard, a comparison of the written position description with the classification standard, and a comparison of the performed duties with the written position description.
The results of this study were the first data available and provide a base for future comparative studies. Over one position in six of those examined was judged to be misclassified, and five of the six were overclassified, and that, of course, means overpaid. Let me quote from the report:
The sample data indicate that throughout the public service there is a distinct tendency to overclassify. This suggests that misclassification does not occur by a simple erroneous application of the classification standard which would likely result in about the same number of positions overclassified as underclassified. It appears that there are motivational and environmental factors within the classification program which encourage overclassification.
The incumbent is not performing the duties described in the job description and a significant cause for misclassification is the misapplication of the classification standard. In this study the possible net salary cost of misclassification was estimated at $43,600,000 per annum.
On February 26, 1976, a report was tabled by me in this House resulting from some 18 months work in what was popularly known as the Finkelman committee, or more properly the Special Joint Committee on Employer-Employee Relations in the Public Service. Under the heading "Classification", eight recommendations are listed. Has any action been taken in the intervening four years?
The report on the classification audit is a cross section of the public service excepting, as it does, the postal groups. Thus we can get no impression of the effectiveness of manuals issued for selective groups. I have in my hands one of these that runs to some 200 pages, or so, which is entitled "Classification and Selection Standard, Scientific Regulation, Scientific and Professional Category". It cost, when it was issued in October 1974, $9.75, obtainable from the Department of Supply and Services. I will read two short paragraphs, if I may:
This standard describes the plan to be used in classifying and evaluating positions in the Scientific Regulation Group, and in selecting personnel for appointment to them.
The second paragraph reads:
The Scientific and Professional Category is composed of occupational groups engaged in the application of the comprehensive body of knowledge acquired through university graduation in fields specified in the group definitions, and of professional groups in which membership in Canada is generally controlled by legally established licensing bodies.
Of course, the point here is that this is quite a sizeable document for what is quite a small segment of the public
Classification Audit
service. I have no idea whether similar documents are produced for every sector, but that in itself is a pretty good base on which to be working. That was issued in 1974. This first report to which I am referring, the one that appears in the motion, is now some two years old.
In February of 1979, just over a year ago, the then president of the treasury board produced an impressive document entitled "Program Performance Measurements". 1 wonder, and I think I have a right to wonder, just how you measure the performance of a person who is both overclassified and overpaid.
In March of 1979, the final report of the royal commission on financial management and accountability was issued. This report, commonly known as the Lambert commission report, is a most interesting document into which not only was a tremendous amount of work put but in regard to which there has been a considerable number of seminars and studies conducted since its issuance. Of course, it deals in part with the subject of classification which we are debating this afternoon.
The question-and it is the same question I am putting all the time-is: What action has been taken since the issuance of the report? I should refer also to the fact that that report runs to some 586 pages and costs $8.50 per book, whether it is the French or English edition. In September of last year we received a 259 page report entitled "The Report of the Special Committee on the Review of Personnel Management and the Merit Principle." This report, popularly known as the D'Avig-non report, runs to some 291 pages in French and was issued at a cost of $10.
When I put motions such as this on the order paper, 1 am trying to underline a point which I have been trying to underline since I came here some eight years ago. I would like the government to tell us just what progress has been made, at what stage we are at, what has happened since the issuance of the report which is the subject of the motion, what has been done with all the recommendations in the Finkelman report to which I referred earlier and which was tabled several years ago, and on which personally I have heard nothing regarding the progress and implementation of the many recommendations in it, recommendations, incidentally, which I can say were almost unanimous.
I think that hon. members present in the House would not dispute my saying that that report was almost unanimous. But we have heard nothing and there has been no subsequent report and no subsequent reference, and therefore no subsequent study on implementation. I can say that the same thing applies to the Lambert commission report and the D'Avignon report.
My motion is therefore a plea to the government to look at some means by which we can be better informed. May I suggest that one of the best ways in which we could be informed is by making it possible for us to study the subject in committee? Of course, we need a reference. There are many

May 29, 1980
Classification Audit
other matters being referred to committee at the present time, but surely efficiency in the public service should be a priority.
The motion was turned down by the government because the wording might not have been precisely correct. After all, we do not always know enough to know precisely what to ask for, and as a result the motion was turned down. I am not taking particular issue with that; I am only saying that it did give me the opportunity to say a few words on the subject of classification in the public service. I should like to include in that general plea a request that an opportunity be given for discussion of whatever progress might or might not have been made as a result of the production of these numerous reports to which I have referred in my remarks.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Daudlin (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION AUDIT REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to thank the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) for bringing this matter forward for debate, notwithstanding the fact that I am sure he shares with me some disappointment in not being able to have the specifics for which he originally made his request. He has indicated his understanding that the base which he sought does not exist. I share with him the interest he has in the entire question of classification, as I am sure many hon. members in this House do, particularly those who have sat on the committees to which he referred, in particular the Finkel-man committee upon which both he and I and other members whom I see present in the House have sat and have laboured so diligently.
Notwithstanding the fact that that information does not exist-and the hon. member was so advised-it is good that we at least discuss the subject matter today, in order perhaps that we get on the record and clarify for the sake of hon. members here today how far we have been able to progress, and indeed what is the current state of conditions with respect to the concept of classifications.
1 should like to refer as well to the three reports which the hon. member has mentioned-the Lambert commission report, the D'Avignon report and the Finkelman report-and I would like to advise him that all of these reports are currently under intensive study at the level of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston). He is requesting on a bi-weekly basis to be updated with respect to those studies so that implementation can be achieved at a fairly early date of at least some of the recommendations that have been made in those reports so that there can be some results obtained from the work that went into them.
The present classification system in the Public Service of Canada was developed in accordance with recommendations made in 1965 by the preparatory committee on collective bargaining. At that time, the committee concluded that a new classification system should have the following objectives.
The first objective is to bring together civil servants and prevailing rate employees under one system; second, to be flexible enough to meet both the demands of the labour market and those of internal relativity; third, to provide a logical framework for the determination of bargaining units and the
negotiation of pay rates; fourth, to permit different approaches to wage and salary administration and to personnel administration generally, for different types of employees; fifth, to be conducive to effective career planning and development and to provide strong incentives to superior performance; and sixth, to permit extensive delegation to departments of the authority to classify positions.
The preparatory committee concluded that these objectives could be achieved by developing a system based on the principle of occupational grouping. The resulting system, which is in use now, was designed to have the following features.
The first is to provide a logical framework for comparing and ranking positions within an occupational group; the second, to provide a means by which a series of positions within a particular group can be compared to each other and to similar occupations in the non-federal public service and the private sector for the purposes of establishing salary relativity for collective bargaining; the third, to permit the establishment of a basis on which the employer is able to attract and retain employees, that is, against which appropriate rates of remuneration can be established for the specific job responsibilities, and periodically revised; the fourth, to permit the identification of the skills, aptitudes and abilities required of the incumbent in a position; the fifth, to permit the establishment of a career structure for clusters of employees; the sixth, to provide the means by which the employer, the employee and the bargaining agent can achieve a common understanding of what management wants done and what is therefore expected of the employee; and the seventh, to provide the means by which the over-all organizational role or objective can be divided into individual position responsibilities.
While the classification system was designed to have the foregoing features, in itself it is intended to do nothing more than establish the basic level of responsibility for the duties of a position and the relativity, within an occupational group, of one position to another.
At present, occupations are divided into six broad categories, with 183 groups and subgroups within these categories. The occupational category is a family of occupations related in broad terms by the nature of the functions fulfilled and by the extent of academic preparation needed by people engaged in these occupations.
The six occupational categories to which I referred earlier are as follows. The first is the occupational category which includes the groups in which manual and related work of an unskilled, semi-skilled or a skilled nature is performed and supervised.
The second is the administrative support category, including the groups in which the preparation, transferring, systematizing and maintenance of records, reports and communications, or the direct application of rules and regulations, or the supervision of these functions are performed.
The third is the technical category, including groups in which specialized techniques are performed that require highly
May 29, 1980

developed skills and a defined minimum of secondary school education.
The fourth is the administrative and foreign service category, including the groups engaged in planning, execution, conduct and control of programs, including those directed toward the public and programs of internal management.
The fifth is the scientific and professional category composed of groups in which specialized qualifications attained in university or professional institutions and specific to each occupational group are required.
Finally, the executive category is composed of groups engaged in senior managerial and policy-making responsibilities, or in tasks calling for exceptionally high standards of performance in the development and execution of policy, or in the introduction of new or improved administrative processes.
Classification is basically a judgment process by which a rank order-for example a relative worth-of a series of positions is established. In a small, simple organization, this ranking may be based on nothing more than the perception of the manager. At the other extreme, such as in the case of the public service, where classification authority is extensively delegated and the classification systems cover an extremely large and diverse work force, a highly sophisticated system is obviously required.
Therefore, public service classification standards exist to ensure that judgments are based on common and consistent criteria, and that the relative worth of a position can be established not only in relation to other positions in a group within the organization or department, but also in relation to positions in the same group in other departments and agencies.
There are four basic types of evaluation plans currently in use in the federal public service. It would probably do us some service to explore, at least briefly, those four groups. The first is the ranking system. These types of evaluation plans are used where there is a high degree of homogeneity in an occupational group and a limited number of different types of work situations. Usually there is already an established and understood job hierarchy in such occupations. An example of this type might be the law group. The second is the level description which is a refinement of the ranking system. It is used when most of the same conditions as in the ranking system apply but a greater variety of work situations exist. By way of example one could look at the engineering subgroup.
The third is the so-called predominant factor system. This type of evaluation plan is used when an occupational group has common characteristics, but a variety of work situations exist which cannot be easily related to each other on the basis of a direct job to job comparison. An example of this type might be the commerce group.	.
Finally, the point rating plan. This type of evaluation plan is used when a high degree of heterogeneity exists among jobs in the same occupations to the extent that neither qualifications nor work situations can be compared easily one with the other. An example of this would be program administration.
Classification Audit
The classification system I have been describing has now been in use for 13 years, and from time to time in recent years the question has been raised as to whether it is still appropriate for the 1980s or whether it should be changed from one based on occupational groups to one based on departments, or to other approaches such as a classification index or centralized classification system.
Under a departmental system, one or more departmental groups would be established which could recognize departmental relativities but would ignore interdepartmental relativities. A similar system existed prior to 1965. Flowever, the present public service classification system is based on the premise that most jobs are similar across the service and there are very few occupational groups which are unique to individual departments. The current approach encourages and facilitates interdepartmental mobility.
A departmental system would solve the problem of intradepartmental relativities, but would not lead to over-all improvement. The extensive administrative exercise required to make such a transition would be traumatic, while the cost of such a change-over is prohibitive. The system would introduce equity problems and would require changes in the Public Service Staff Relations Act and a restructuring of the bargaining units.
The provinces have a variety of systems and practices depending on the size and complexity of their public service work force. Where collective bargaining is permitted, there are fewer bargaining units than are found in the federal public service. As well, classification delegation is far more restricted. Generally, according to provincial authorities, control problems exist wherever classification delegation is permitted.
In the Canadian private sector, classification systems range from ones which are far simpler than those of the federal public service to ones which are equally complex. The degree of complexity generally increases with the size of the enterprise and its geographical dispersion. For example, in the grain industry there is a high degree of consistency between companies and the classification system is very simple.
In a number of companies, for jobs which would be allocated to groups in our operational and technical categories, no formal classification plan exists and job descriptions are very basic. Again I offer as an example the electrician whose job classification is to supervise all electrical work, to assign staff their duties and to perform electrical-related work as required.
At the other extreme, the steel industry uses a system, the co-operative wage study evaluation system or CWS, covering thousands of plants and office workers in the United States and Canada. Two classification plans, a 12-factor plan for blue collar workers and a seven-factor plan for office workers, are used. Despite access to a grievance procedure, including provision for final and binding arbitration in the event that union-management agreement is not reached and revisions that have been periodically incorporated in the 35-year history of this old plan, steel unions have recently gone on record as considering that significant modifications are required to the CWS classification plan.

May 29, 1980
Classification Audit
In the private sector there is usually a distinct split between managers and others, whereas in the public service classification plans a complete spectrum of work from most junior to intermediate or senior management level is covered. As well, our plans, except for senior executives or the SXs as they are called and personnel administration, the PE positions, normally cover both unionized and excluded employees. Private sector ones do not and the demarcation is much more distinct. Management levels in significant private sector organizations are usually covered by direct or partial reference to compensation systems developed by consultant organizations.
Generally in the private sector both personnel administration and classification are highly centralized. Where there is a measure of delegation, this is usually exercised under tight guidelines which leave very little room for discretion on the part of the manager. In effect, the manager establishes a position by selecting one of a series of job descriptions that has been developed at the corporate level. Because the diversity of work and programs in the public service rarely exists within one company in the private sector, more centralized and straightforward approaches to classification are possible in the private sector.
In the United States, at the federal level the classification system, commonly known as the GS system, closely approximates our class and grade system which existed prior to the introduction of collective bargaining. There are a large number of series and grades in existence for the clerical through officer classes of work. These grades in turn are assigned to one of some 18 GS pay levels. Thus, a biologist, a chemist and an administrative officer, although classified in their own distinct classification series, could all be paid in the same GS pay level. The introduction of a similar system in the Canadian federal public service would require a revamping of the entire existing bargaining unit structure to allow the negotiation of a unified rate structure for all occupational groups.
Another difference in the American system is that while delegation is permitted, collective bargaining is restricted or prohibited. While the pay system is simpler, there are a number of problems in the classification area and studies have been under way to reform the system.

speechtext:
I am glad that hon. members are happy to see that the studies are under way. I commenced my speech by indicating that the studies are under way. As any good teacher would do, having started with the point, I am reinforcing the point through the middle of the speech and I will conclude with the same point.
As is evident from the foregoing, the current American classification system and classification in the private sector operate in a significantly different and highly varied arena. The systems used range from those which would be totally incompatible with our organizational structure to ones which
are comparable and, except for the cosmetic differences, essentially the same.
In conclusion, I have endeavoured to describe the particulars of the current classification system in the public service. As I have indicated, it is a complex system, but I assure hon. members that the classification policies and procedures are under constant review to maintain a system that is fair to both employees and taxpayers.
The President of the Treasury Board, 1 believe, has indicated in this House and, therefore, publicly, and privately to many hon. members who have an interest in this topic, as has the hon. member for Vaudreuil, that he has a personal commitment to see that these three reports to which I referred earlier do not languish in the dust on the shelf, that they in fact receive a complete examination and that that examination results in some action in terms of the implementation of at least parts of those reports.
It is a commitment on the part of the President of the Treasury Board that this be done quickly and effectively, and that in fact it should be done in the context of changes in the PSSRA legislation which obviously will have to come forward. I would ask the assistance and co-operation of all members of this House to see that this matter is dealt with quickly.
I agree with the hon. member for Vaudreuil when he says that this has been a matter of long standing and that it requires that something effective be done soon in consultation not only with members of this House but with members of the public service who, obviously, are vitally interested and concerned and who will be affected by what happens.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION AUDIT REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) for giving us this evening the opportunity of discussing a topic that although not of the easiest to understand, still concerns a subject of interest to at least some hon. members and also to the House generally because, in the final analysis, Parliament is responsible for the management of human resources. This question of job classification and its standards is inevitably linked with the whole question of human resource management and civil servants.
I heard the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of Treasury Board (Mr. Daudlin) indicate some of the steps that have been taken to ensure that in a few months, if not sooner, solutions will be brought to the problems pointed out by my colleague from Vaudreuil. I would remind the parliamentary secretary and his minister that we have been impatiently waiting for four years already for the results of the study made in 1976 by a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate on employer-employee relations in the civil service of Canada. That study which, I believe, was presided over by the hon. member for Vaudreuil some time ago recommended that classification be made negotiable and that, of course, certain conditions attach to the application of the new formula.
May 29, 1980

Job classification is, put simply, the first step toward filling a position. The manager must, in fact, determine the parameters of the job, evaluate the work to be performed and, after analysis, locate that position at the appropriate level in the general classification scale. The level of classification having been determinated, the Civil Service Commission is then asked to set the selection standards. So, on one hand the employer has the exclusive right to determine the classification standards, the work to be done. The employer decides what will happen. On the other hand, the Public Service Commission must by law choose the candidate who seems best qualified to fill the position. Therefore, on one hand we have the employer who must identify the work to be done and on the other hand we have an agency which must find the person best suited for the work.
As we can see, classification represents one important part of the management of our human resources in the civil service. According to the law now in force, the employer unilaterally decides on the classification standards, though ordinarily a consultation process takes place between negotiating agents. Normally, before applying or changing any standard, the Treasury Board consults with the negotiating agents.
In the public sector, as my colleague the parliamentary secretary to the minister has mentioned, it is different, even in the United States. Four years ago I thought we were slowly on the way to adopting a much more modern system, that the employer, although he may be completely in charge of setting the classification standards, would have understood that his task was an integral part of personnel management and that if classification meant money-if I hold a senior position, I am well paid and if the salary is negotiable-it necessarily follows that classification should also be negotiable. 1 negotiate with respect to salary so I should therefore negotiate with respect to classification.
This is what the employer-employee relations committee which met in 1974, 1975 and 1976 recommended; and 1 will simply read an excerpt for hon. members because this document has gathered a lot of dust in the last four years. Its recommendations were never followed up and I would simply like to remind hon. members of what the House and Senate committee recommended. I quote from page 4721:
Your committee is of the opinion that the law should provide for some extension of the scope of bargaining so as to include classification standards, and recommends as follows:
34.	That, having regard to the established jurisdiction of bargaining agents in the public service, bargaining classification standards be interpreted to mean the determination of the relative worth of jobs within an occupational group.
35.	That provision be made in the law for the bargaining of classification standards following the three-year period after promulgation.
36.	That collective agreements incorporating classification standards be treated as "special agreements having their own duration".
Classification Audit
37.	That in accordance with regulations made by the Public Service Staff Relations Board, disputes arising in negotiations and involving the development or redevelopment of a classification standard be subject to reference to and arbitration by the Board.
38.	That the provisions of the act relating to the appointment of conciliation boards or conciliators not apply in cases of disputes arising out of the negotiations of classification standards, but that the board be empowered to appoint a mediator.
39.	That resort to strike or lockout to resolve classification disputes be prohibited.
40.	That arbitration of the pay plan attached to a classification standard be dealt with by the Public Service Staff Relations Board only with the consent of both parties.
As we can see, Mr. Speaker, four years ago members of this House made seven recommendations on how, in a clear and precise manner and step by step, standards of classification could become negotiable just as salaries and other working conditions are negotiable. This brings us back to the problem raised by the hon. member for Vaudreuil. Four years ago it was realized, according to the report under study today and which is the basis for this motion for the production of papers, that the issue of classification audit in the public service posed certain problems. That report indicated certain positions were overclassified or underclassified, overpaid or underpaid. And I remember at that time, four years ago, that document was alluded to and it was said once again that civil servants receive more money than they deserve and do work that bring them working conditions and salaries that far exceed what they are worth. Mr. Macdonell, the Auditor General, recently told us that federal civil servants were for a large part unable to do their work with the same efficiency and effectiveness as the private sector. We were told that 50,000 federal civil servants could do the job as effectively as 36,000 comparable workers in the private sector. And that was used to hit again civil servants over the head and tell them: Listen, you are overpaid, there is not enough strictness to prevent those abuses. And the press jumped on that.
I must say that classification is determined by the employer, who is also responsible for personnel management. And when one talks about the efficiency of federal civil servants, one should not forget that it is management, and in the final analysis the agencies themselves, and perhaps this Parliament, that is responsible for that. Because we did not make sure we had the controls we needed, we did not make sure for many years we had in place a necessary approach to management so the managers could administer their departments effectively.
And then the civil servant gets blamed-that happened four years ago when the report on classification was released, and again recently when the Auditor General acted on a very doubtful basis. Mr. Speaker, 160 civil servants were extrapolated on 50,000, and that is what the Auditor General based himself on to conclude there was a lack of effectiveness and efficiency in the public service. What the hon. member for Vaudreuil sought is to get-

May 29, 1980
Classification Audit

We are told that the data behind this study is unavailable. I accept that. Possibly it did not exist. I do not know, but somebody made a statement that 17.8 per cent of public servants in the national capital area were overclassified, and somebody made a statement also that outside the national capital area it was a lower percentage than the national capital area but, nevertheless, an important percentage were overclassified. In both instances I claim this is not the fault of the public servants; it is the fault of the system. On the one hand, we do not have a general policy, a philosophy of management, and on the other hand classification is the employer's exclusive responsibility. Perhaps some day we can set up a system which will give the employees and the unions a chance to negotiate classification standards.
The problem, of course, arises when we divide normal negotiations on standard things such as salary and fringe benefits like health, pensions and such things. Some of them are accepted as part of normal negotiations today. In our report, in the D'Avignon report and the Lambert report for that matter, it is suggested that the staffing process be part of another type of negotiation, separate from the normal negotiations going on regarding salaries and other conditions.
I see some difficulties with that. If the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of Treasury Board is serious, I want to warn him that there may be some difficulties inherent in double negotiations-on the one hand negotiating salaries and conditions of work and, on the other hand, negotiating staffing and classification standards. A contract signed for a period of time covering salaries and working conditions may be arrived at in the next month or so, but a contract in regard to classification standards and staffing functions may be effective only next year. The process of negotiation would then start over again and the public service and the government would find themselves negotiating pretty well all the time on two different contracts, one dealing with money and other conditions, and one dealing with classification and staffing. I would caution the parliamentary secretary about that. Two negotiations going on at parallel times could complicate the whole process and add to the complexities of the problem.
I should like to talk now about the classification question. For the past several years Treasury Board has carried out ad hoc audits of departmental classification decisions, and has taken the necessary corrective action. I accept that they cannot audit everybody all the time. They audit some medium and large departments every 18 months, and I understand that they audit small departments, boards and agencies, every 24 months. Although this provides information about the administration of various aspects of the system, the subjective selection of position used does not allow quantitative statements about classification for particular departments in the whole public service.
When these audits revealed possible problems with the classification system as a whole, it was decided to carry out a full scale audit. A full scale audit is required if we are ever to come to grips with the management philosophy-the over-all
responsibility of this Parliament, this government-to make sure that we reach effective goals in administering public funds and that we obtain efficient services and value for money from our taxes.
I understand that the evaluation and analysis made in 1976 was done in consultation with Statistics Canada. The method automatically ensured that departments and occupational groups were represented in this sample. In the national capital area, one of every 33 positions was selected. That is what we call the subjective approach system. In the non-national capital area, one out of every 69 positions was selected. Here again we are taking advice from professional statisticians and trying to cope with a very challenging problem but doing it with well recognized scientific methods.
The application of the staffing method resulted in approximately 2,000 positions being selected in the national capital region, which represented approximately 4 per cent of the full-time employees who had been in the same job for over 12 months. After completion of the national capital area phase of the program, the audit was repeated for another 2,000 positions in the rest of Canada outside the national capital area, to substantiate further and expand the results of the study in the national capital area. This sample represented approximately 1.5 per cent of full-time employees outside the national capital area. The combined results of these two phases provided the assessment of the entire public service.
I am not much of a statistician, Mr. Speaker. I know nothing about statistics and have never taken such a course. I suspect, however, that we are in a situation similar to the one the Auditor General was in when he apparently used 160 public servants out of 50,000 and, from that, extrapolated the finding that they were not efficient. I do not know how acceptable that is to the ordinary person. I find it difficult to accept that we can extrapolate 160 to 50,000 and that we can extrapolate from 1.5 per cent of full-time employees outside the national capital area and say there is great difficulty here in classification standards.
[DOT] <1750)
The systematic audit of 4,000 positions in the public service showed that a significant percentage of positions were misclas-sified, I quote from the document, both inside and outside the national capital area. The NCA was 20 per cent, while in the non-NCA-that is the non-capital area-it was 16.7 per cent. For the public service as a whole, the percentage of misclassi-fied positions was 17.8 per cent.
I would like to point out that there will always be some subjectivity in the administration of any classification system. There will always be some cases where the duties and responsibilities of the particular position could be at the lower end of one particular classification level, or at the upper end of a lower level. Because of this, and because of the size and nature of the classification system in the federal public service-the system covers, I understand, about 300,000 positions-there will always be some degree of misclassification. That is acceptable in as big a shop as that employing 300,000 people and it is
May 29, 1980

expected that there would be movements up and down and some misclassification. But in the order of 20 per cent-the extrapolation that has been done-if it is right, it is in dire need of change, and it is wrong, it is in great need of being readjusted. That is possibly why the hon. member for Vau-dreuil wanted to see the data that produced these figures so that we could understand where the problems were.
As a result of the initial findings of the audits in the national capital area, departments were advised of the general results of the audit while the Treasury Board continued with the audit outside the national capital area. In addition, the Treasury Board undertook a thorough study of the classification system in the personnel policy branch of Treasury Board and one other operating department, as well as a detailed review of all the policies and procedures relating to classification in the public service. They reviewed the policies and procedures.

Classification audits such as the national capital and the non-national capital audits which were referred to by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, have found that some positions are either overclassified or underclassified, that is, the pay for the actual duties being performed is not consistent with that for similar positions elsewhere in the public service.
It is evident that corrective action is necessary in such situations. Where a position is underclassified, the employee immediately receives the benefit of the higher salary, which is just. If, and looking at the position in the first instance, we find that a man or woman because of the job they are doing is underpaid, then it is incumbent upon the employer to see to it that they are justly remunerated for the work they are doing.
In cases of overclassification, the process known as red circling is somewhat different. It is to this point that 1 wish to address myself. In the mid-1960s, with the introduction of the present category and group classification system, mentioned by my colleague, the hon. member for Essex-Kent, who referred to a study which was carried out in the United States, we found that the employer provided for corrective action, generally resulting in a freeze of the employee's salary for 60 or 90 days after notification of the overclassification situation. That was done unless-and this is very important-the position could be restructured to sustain the overclassified level. This freeze was to continue until the salary for the correct classification level coincided with the employee's frozen rate of pay. The employee suffered no monetary loss. My colleague from Timmins knows that from his studies and from the people working in his riding-we discussed this a little bit earlier- this was a very important aspect for them as it bore directly on the well-being of their families as well as on colleagues working in the same offices.
As 1 said before, the employees suffered no monetary loss. But later, to protect the red circled employees from adverse effects of increases in the cost of living, lump sum payments were instituted. In their time, these red circling provisions were at least equal to corrective classification provisions of other employees.

The Battlefords-Meadow Lake constituency is located in northwestern Saskatchewan and geographically covers about a quarter of the entire size of the province of Saskatchewan. It stretches from the Borden Bridge in the southeastern corner of the constituency, along the North Saskatchewan River to the Alberta border, and north to the Northwest Territories, taking in communities such as Meadow Lake, The Battlefords, as 1 already mentioned Buffalo Narrows, and Uranium City in the extreme northern corner of the constituency.
The constituency has a fairly diverse economy. Its economic base originally has been mainly agriculture, and fishing and trapping as we move further north out of the agricultural areas. Agriculture has been and likely in the long term will always be the number one industry within The Battlefords-Meadow Lake constituency, although it is a bit overshadowed at the present time because of heavy oil development, some manufacturing and mining, and an equitable distribution of income from a sound resource policy of the government that we have in Saskatchewan, as well as extensive forestry operations which take place within the constituency. However, they have been devastated somewhat recently because of the numerous forest fires of such a large extent that have been experienced in northern Saskatchewan and throughout all of northern Canada.
The constituency has a rich cultural background of Ukrainian people, people of Scandinavian ancestry, German, French, British, and in the largest part of the constituency we actually represent people from all countries in the world. As well, about 45 per cent of the constituency is made up of native people. Here I speak of treaty Indians, the registered Indians, nonstatus Indians and the Metis people who live within the constituency.
As you are well aware, Mr. Speaker, we have an NDP government which has been in power since 1971. It has done a very good job of providing the people of Saskatchewan with a good diverse economy. Mr. Speaker, in joining in this debate, on Bill C-30 tonight, which 1 remind hon. members of the House and the public is a bill in which the government is requesting authority to borrow a further $12 billion, 1 feel it might be helpful, first of all, to try to put that sum into perspective. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I believe we in this House often lose total sight of the figures with which we are dealing.
As a result of the government's borrowing needs, they are now required to pay something like 12 per cent interest per year when they borrow money. To put that into perspective, as we debate tonight this small bill, large in its impact, remember that with interest rates running at 12 per cent, money on a cumulative basis doubles in six years and goes up four times in 12 years. This means that we are not in fact talking about $12 billion, we are talking about the creation of debt in the name of Canada that will require, over the next six years, a further $12 billion simply to service it. Then 12 years ahead, the total amount of debt and servicing charges that will be required is $48 billion and within 18 years it is then, of course, $96 billion.
The reason I emphasize this, Mr. Speaker, is that 1 am so totally and unbelievably shocked by the indifference of this government to the magnitude of what they have asked this House to do by introducing this bill.
To put it again into perspective, once I was told by a bureaucrat, when there was a little uncertainty as to whether he meant in the case of this deal, $10 million or $10 billion, that we never use the last three digits in Ottawa. That is part

May 29, 1980
Borrowing Authority Act
of this nation's problem, Mr. Speaker. We have had a government for the last decade especially, with the brief interregnum, that frankly does not relate to the figures they are forcing the Canadian public to accept.
It is easy to do the arithmetic. What we are considering tonight, in effect, is whether the government should be empowered to go out and, on behalf of every man, woman and child in Canada, borrow $500. That is what we are talking about. For a family of three we are being asked to allow the government to go out and borrow $1,500. It is as simple as that. With interest at 12 per cent and applying the cumulative factor, that means that for every man, woman and child we are, in effect, going to incur a debt of $500 on their behalf, that becomes $1,000 in six years, $2,000 in 12 years and $4,000 in 18 years. This does not have to continue, Mr. Speaker. With a responsible government, a government that is willing to attempt to balance its budgetary position, this ongoing increase first, of budgetary deficits and second, of debt requirements, could be halted.
I was rather encouraged as 1 came into the House tonight to hear the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish) at least showing some alarm with respect to what we are being asked to consider and approve tonight. 1 think it is good that any member of the House, whether he be socialist, Liberal or Conservative, has the courage to stand up and say, "We have had enough of this and we are not going to rubberstamp it any further."
I know it is commonplace for this government that believes only in political power, is totally indifferent to the economic consequence of its actions, to say, "Maybe things are not as good as we would like in Canada but, after all, we are not doing badly compared with other countries." In that connection, let me refer to a couple of things. In the Spring 1980 Review, the Friedberg Mercantile Group have an interesting chart in which they set out the comparative CPI figures, the wholesale increase figures, and the current account positions with respect to ten of the most industrialized nations in the world. If hon. members think that Canada is not doing too badly, I ask them to please take a look at these charts.

The first chart deals with the consumer price index. It ranks Canada sixth among the ten. The next chart deals with wholesale prices and it ranks Canada ninth out of ten; only one country is worse, and that is Italy. With regard to our current account deficit, we have the distinction of being the last. We are the ninth worst in the industrialized world. There were no figures for the tenth country to show how it performed.
Somehow this is all knitted together. I know that members on the government side might be quick to say that is just one economist's or company's views, but let me quote their own figures to them. Earlier this week the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen)-who I am quite disappointed is not in the House tonight while this bill is being considered-tabled his Economic Review. Again, I invite all members to leaf through that review because it they do not want to accept the figures
that may be put on the record from this side of the House, surely they will accept the figures from their own Minister of Finance.
For example, what that review highlights is the tremendous imbalance of taxation in this country compared to that of the United States. I refer to page 136 of the review, table 11.22. That shows a Canada-United States comparison of government expenditures by function as a percentage of their gross national product. I emphasize that this is not dealing with simple dollar terms, it is dealing in the percentages being spent in those two countries in relation to their respective gross national products.
In the case of the United States, it shows that the total expenditure in that country is 34.6 per cent of its gross national product. That is the expenditure on account of government. In Canada, the expenditure is 41.8 per cent. As one can see, it is over 7 per cent higher, and it is over 20 per cent higher, if you want to take one percentage over another, than that in the United States. That is onlv part of the story, Mr. Speaker.
You will find the reason that the American figures are as high as they are is that they are spending 5.4 per cent of their gross national product on defence, while Canada is spending only 1.7 per cent. If those figures are equalized, and if the Americans, for example, only spent on defence-and I am not suggesting that they should-what we are spending relatively, it would mean that their total governmental expenditures are 30.9 per cent compared to Canada's 41.8 per cent.
I refer to that because sometimes we lose sight of the fact that in Canada we have not only become one of the most over-governed countries in the world, we have become one of the most inefficient, expensive countries in the world as far as government is concerned. This is so significant because the figures that I have given are comparative figures to those of the United States.
The Americans are our main trading partners. It is the United States that holds out the greatest hope for further exports as far as Canada is concerned. I can only tell hon. members, Mr. Speaker, to the degree that we are loading our Canadian public with approximately 20 per cent more in government expenditures, that we are handicapping our people in their productivity and in other means of exploiting that American market.
That brings me to the discounted dollar, because the two are related. As hon. members are undoubtedly aware, we had to let our dollar fall because we could no longer compete on the world markets with a dollar roughly at part with the United States. One reason why we could not compete was because we had loaded our workers with this excess government spending which meant extra taxation on their backs compared to their counterparts in the United States. The phony equalization mechanism is simply to allow the dollar to fall, roughly 15 per cent, which then makes the Canadian worker a person working for 15 per cent less than he used to work for in terms of American dollars. That is what happened with a discounted Canadian dollar. We require every worker in Canada in terms

of American dollars to simply take a pay cut of over 15 per cent in order to allow the Liberal government to continue with its high-flying spending approaches.

For example, there is an international comparison of central government expenditures on page 135 of the review at Table 11.21. It is interesting to note that there is only one country that has a higher central government expenditure than Canada. Guess who? It is Italy. That is the only country. Australia has a total expenditure of 29.7 per cent. I could read the whole list into the record. Again, it is interesting to note that as far as international comparisons of central budget balances are concerned, again, in 1977, those are the last available figures, there is only one country worse than Canada, and that is Italy.
Again, most importantly, when we compare the budgetary deficit in Canada for 1979 with that of the United States- and these figures are available on page 133, Table 11.19 of that Economic Review-I am pleased that you are seated, Mr. Speaker, because how many people in Canada realize that while these Grits have led us to the position of where we have a deficit in relation to our gross national product of 3.5 per cent, the Americans are virtually in balance with minus 0.4 per cent in relation to their GNP? These are the facts.
I believe it is particularly relevant tonight to be putting those facts on the record as we consider a bill in which the government is asking us to approve it borrowing, on behalf of every man, woman and child in this country, an extra $500.
Think what this government has done to interest rates in the country. There seems to be great confusion about this. I have heard our socialist friends to the left stand up and say, "Reduce interest rates" and the next speaker will stand up and say that certain expenditures should be increased as far as the government is concerned, without realizing that if you increase expenditures with a government that is already spending one-third more than its revenue, you have no place to cover your expenditure other than going into debt further which drives up interest rates.
Let me again refer to the Economic Review of the Minister of Finance. What they have loaded Canada with is all spelled out. For example, on page 141 of that review there is a chart which indicates that in 1970-73, interest rates in Canada at one time were actually below 6 per cent. That is as recently as the 1970-73 time-frame.
In 1974-77 they got up as high as 9 per cent. In 1978 they were almost continually above 9 per cent. In 1979 they got up to almost 11 per cent, certainly over 10 per cent. As we know, recently interest rates on Canadian government bonds got as high as 13% per cent. This is the bottom line, if you like, of the inept bungling on the part of the present government.

I would like to refer, and perhaps read into the record because it is so interesting, what the Economic Review says concerning comparative interest rate levels at the federal government level and the provincial level in Canada. Referring to page 141 of the Minister of Finance's own Economic Review, it states:
While there may not be a close relationship between nominal interest rates and total borrowing requirements, relative yields within the Canadian financial markets have been influenced over the past decade by the relative volumes of securities available. For example, the yield on federal securities has increased relative to the yields on comparable private sector securities over the course of the decade as the federal government increased its marketable issues at a rapid pace. Thus, while federal government marketable bonds represented 20 per cent of the Canadian dollar bond holdings of the general public in 1970 and almost 25 per cent in 1979, the yield differential between federal and provincial bonds dropped from 1.13 percentage points in 1970 to 0.53 points in 1979, and the spread between federal bonds and comparable private securities narrowed over the same period from 1.27 to 0.69 percentage points. A similar situation occurred in the short-term money market where the federal government's securities constituted less than 4 per cent of the market in 1970 and more than 10 per cent in 1979.
Expressed simply, what that review, or the economist who wrote that paragraph, is saying is that the federal government, which used to be able to borrow money at over one percentage point less than the provinces in Canada, has now borrowed money to such excess that that differential has been cut by more than half. That is significant.

Unless the present government arrests the trend, that is the net position as far as expenditures and revenues are concerned. The net cumulative

deficit will be increased by $27 billion if the Minister of Finance does not come up with something comparable to what we proposed on December 11 to narrow the deficit in this country.

Under the budget that we proposed, by 1984, with the restraint that we proposed, and with the revenue increases that we suggested, the total net debt position would be $105 billion. Without that budget, and as the trend is now in place, the net debt will be $133 billion.
Let me put that into per capita terms. It will mean there will be approximately $1,200 of added debt over and above what we would have suggested for every man, woman and child in this country. If there is any compassion in these ruthless, hungry political people who somehow or other covet power over everything else, surely they are going to bring a halt to this type of extravagant expenditure performance that has been their tradition in Canada.
It is so typical of the government now ruling this country for me to be able to look across the aisle and see the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) giggling and laughing as if this is one of the funniest things that has ever happened in the nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-30, an act to provide supplementary borrowing authority for the fiscal year 198081. I do so because the wording of the bill and the minister's introduction to it on May 27 raise more questions than they answer. In fact the minister's speech is surely a model of brevity. When he wrote it he must have been looking at the three monkeys. By that I mean the three monkeys that hear no evil, speak no evil, and see no evil. He definitely made certain not to tell the House any more than the barest essentials. In fact, his speech is so naked in content that had it been presented anywhere but in this chamber, I feel that the minister may well have been charged with indecently exposing his borrowing act.
I listened to the minister's speech, I read and reread it, and I did the same thing with Bill C-30. But because it tells me nothing about the government's plans I cannot in all honesty, as the representative of the people of South Shore, vote for this measure. As close as I can determine, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) stood in his place and simply stated that the government needs borrowing authority for $12 billion for the fiscal year 1980-81, in foreign currency as well as in Canadian money. Obviously he has already had a little twinge of concern that he and his colleagues may have gone once too often to the cookie jar and that perhaps the cookie jar may be becoming empty. So now he wants to make certain that he has the right to go to some other country's cookie jar in order to get the funds he may require, if it is necessary. All this may be due to the minister's Scottish background and his ingrained sense of thrift which causes him to make certain that sufficient funds are available from any source for his needs. If this is the case, our only regret is that his sense of thrift is obviously not shared by his colleagues.
The minister also referred to his statement of April 21 when he tabled a projection of the government's budgetary requirements for 1980-81 in the amount of $11,730 million. Since then, however, he has decided he needs a little extra margin of borrowing authority to provide for contingencies. So he is rounding out the figures and he is asking for a blank cheque of $12 billion. Well, the difference between the minister's April forecast and his request in May is $270 million, which is not an insignificant amount seeing that little more than a month separates his two statements. It reminds me-and I go back a few years-of the C. D. Howe statement when that gentleman was prone to ask the question, "What's a million?" Obviously this type of thinking still prevails among the present day Liberals. One would hope that they had learned a lesson
Borrowing Authority Act
because the "what's a million" statement cost them the government at that time.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Now it is "What's a billion?"

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Yes, now it is "What's a billion?" The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) must have been reading my notes because that is exactly what I was going to say.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: He wrote them.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
I am sorry but I have to correct the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). The notes that lie in front of me, sir, for your information, were entirely composed and compiled by me; good, bad, or indifferent, they are my effort.
The $12 billion that is in the bill is not the total story. The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance in his brief remarks told us that the unused borrowing authority which is available for use at any time, and which is being carried forward, amounted to approximately $2.9 billion at the beginning of the fiscal year 1980-81, which is really April 1, April Fool's day. The minister may take us all for April fools, but quite frankly I believe that the Canadian electorate is at least entitled to know what this government planned to do not with $12 billion, but $15 billion. That, as was so adequately described by a previous speaker, is $500 for every man, woman and child in Canada. That is in effect what the government is asking the right to borrow at the present time.
I say this because it is now obvious to everyone that the Canadian financial ship of state, sir, is out of control. You need only look over the years in which the Liberal party has been in power to realize the truth of that statement. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was first elected on June 25, 1968, Canada then had a population somewhat in excess of 20 million people, and according to the record, "How Your Tax Dollar Is Spent", which was put out, I think in 1978 by the then president of the Treasury Board, the Hon. Bud Drury, we read that in 1968 it required less than $10 billion to look after the needs of our people. What has happened in the intervening years? Our population has grown to a little more than 23 million and today we require $58.4 billion, perhaps $60 billion, to look after our needs.
With the exception of a brief period during which my party was in office, unfortunately too brief a period, when we proposed to reduce Canada's deficits, the Liberals had been in power under their present leader for some 12 years. The problems which had been brought about by their mismanagement and deficit financing must be laid squarely at the feet of this present government. The $15 billion borrowing pill might be a little easier to swallow if it was coated with the sugar of explanation, and obviously this can only be done if the government provided this House with a budget.
The minister in his shy, retiring manner has given no indication of when we can anticipate a budget, or what his

May 29, 1980
Borrowing Authority Act
final spending plans are for this fiscal year. Obviously we can only anticipate his reticence as being indicative of something more sinister. I refer to his reticence to come clean. He could be "Mr. Clean" with Canadian taxpayers, but we can only judge his reticence as an indication that worse is yet to come. "Come grow old along with me," says the Minister of Finance, "the worst is yet to be." That is about what we are facing tonight.
This bill is asking for SI2 billion borrowing authority on top of, as I said, almost S3 billion already approved. This means that the total sum of $15 billion will have to be borrowed by the government, or will be available to be borrowed by it to finance its operations and to meet its cash requirements during the current fiscal year. This amount, as I said previously, is more than the minister predicted in May that he and his government required. The increased amount is substantial. When one calculates the interest at current borrowing rates, something like 12 per cent, all of which will have to come from the pockets of individual taxpayers, one will see that the load that must be carried by Canadians to support this spendthrift government is staggering. The $15 billion at 12 per cent means a carrying charge for one year only of $1.8 billion.
Why do you need borrowing authority for $14.9 billion? 1 ask the Minister of Finance that through you, Mr. Speaker. Why do you need that when you stated on April 21 last that your total requirement would be only $11.730 billion? That is $3,170 billion more than his own estimate. When you ask for this much money in excess of requirements you certainly cannot any longer hypocritically keep telling the Canadian people that you are a government of restraint or a party practising restraint. This is the course you have been following, but it is way past the time when you should match your words with concrete action.
On January 11 of this year, for example, Mr. Trudeau campaigned for votes, outlining five general commitments to Canadians which were the echoes of some of the same old, reprinted promises we have heard for the past 12 years.
I ask the government, through you, Mr. Speaker, how does it relate this request for almost $15 billion in borrowing authority with Mr. Trudeau's statement that, if elected, the Liberal government "will manage more vigorously the nation's finances in order to make more effective use of the taxpayer's money?" That is his statement. Is it any wonder that the Canadian electorate today are cynical about promises made by their leaders? That is unfortunate, sir.
On May 31, 1968, in his first campaign, Mr. Trudeau told a Moncton office that his government would spend no more than it earned. On August 3, 1969, he said in Ottawa that a new Liberal government restraint program would bring government spending under control. On February 19, 1973, his finance minister promised government determination to impose restraint on its own spending in order to avoid aggravating inflation.
In the throne speech of September 30, 1974, and in the budget speech of June 23, 1975, the Trudeau government promised spending restraints. When announcing wage and
price controls in October of 1975 Mr. Trudeau promised spending restraints. On October 18, 1976, the Liberal president of the Treasury Board promised spending restraints. On August 1, 1978, Mr. Trudeau went on television to tell the nation his government would cut $2 billion in government spending. This is one of the benefits of being around this esteemed chamber for a few years, you can look back and draw on your own experiences. I recall, having gone through ten campaigns, the many promises that had been made by these people on the other side.
With all this restraint we must ask ourselves why are the Canadian people today groaning under an onerous tax burden which siphons the money away from the private or productive sector of the economy and places it in the public or non-productive sector of the economy, thereby contributing to horrendous inflation, while at the same time building up bureaucracy? The answer is that this government has not kept its promises to restrain spending, for the figures tell an entirely different story.
In the fiscal year before its defeat last May the Liberal government spent six times as much as it did in 1968 when Mr. Trudeau first took office and it ended that year with a deficit of more than $12 billion. It seems to me that the Minister of Finance, stating in less than a whole page of Hansard that he wants borrowing authority for another $12 billion-that is a billion dollars a month, or a thousand million dollars a month-is showing his contempt for Parliament. That is a lot of money. That makes the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources smile. 1 am sure his computerized mind was working that one over, but it is a thousand million dollars a month and we have no explanation whatsoever about the manner in which this vast sum of money is to be spent. When they do this, the government and the Minister of Finance are showing contempt for Parliament.
