subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) has the floor.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1980-81 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Thank you, but my time is somewhat limited. I was saying we are expected to sit here and rubber stamp this measure. This is something 1 cannot do, for the government, by following its present course, is not showing any respect for Parliament or its representatives. 1 ask supporters of the government whether any of them could tell us why the executive should require these vast borrowing powers. Why is the government following a course of action which gives them more than $3 billion in excess padding over and above the minister's stated requirements, requirements which have not been explained in any detail to the House? Is this cushion required to maintain the dollar at current levels if there is new pressure against it on the foreign exchange markets because of the obvious mismanagement of the country's affairs? Or is the cushion needed to blunt and contain the adverse effects on the economy of the slow-down, the recession which unfortunately is already under way? All these questions could be answered if the government had the courage to present the House with a budget.
Why are they seeking this enormous, this tremendous, this scandalous borrowing authority without first presenting a budget to Parliament? It is unfair and unjust to ask anyone in this chamber to vote for this measure in the absence of a budget, since we have no way of knowing what to expect by way of revenues and expenditures or what will be the resulting deficit and cash requirements to be financed by borrowing for the balance of the fiscal year.
It is possible some of us might think differently about this request for authority to borrow $12 billion if the minister would open the door just a bit-just wide enough to give us a little peek at his plans. For example, his party has not been adverse in the past to adopting Conservative proposals. Sometimes the stone which the Liberals rejected becomes the headstone of their party's platform. For example, is he giving any thought to adopting our income-tested refundable energy tax credit of $80 per adult and $30 per child a year phased in over two years for the benefit of lower and middle-income Canadians, the group which is hardest hit by present-day high energy costs? Is the minister giving any thought to introducing our mortgage interest and property tax proposals, or a somewhat similar proposal, which in these periods of high interest rates and high property taxes would go a long way toward easing the burdens on our young and not-so-young home owners?
Is the minister perhaps thinking of assisting our small businesses by recognizing the contribution many wives make toward running the business and allowing them to receive salaries as a deductible business expense? Perhaps the hon. gentleman plans to encourage greater regional development by promoting investment in Atlantic fishing vessels built in Canada. This would be helpful in our area. Possibly the Minister of Finance is even thinking about our farmers and is
Borrowing Authority Act
planning some substantial relief for them from the problems caused by the taxation of capital gains when farmland is sold. These are all measures which might use up some of the billions the minister wants to borrow.
However, if I haven't scored bingo on any of my questions, surely the minister must have a shopping list of his own and surely he must realize, now, that he ought to take the House into his confidence and outline his plans to the Canadian people who, in the final analysis, must foot the bill. It is just possible we may see some action on the Prime Minister's promise in Halifax on June 25 that his party seeks to achieve energy security at a fair price for all Canadians. Among other things he promised there would be "a natural gas pipeline to ensure that all Canadians had access to their resources." Liberals, he said, would take "immediate action to begin negotiations for the construction of a natural gas pipeline to Quebec City and the maritimes." Initially, the line was to carry natural gas east, but when maritime supplies were ready the pipeline would be like a natural gas railroad with a return delivery facility as well. That was the promise. Well, it seems that the National Energy Board ruling has put a stop to that prospect, and the ones being railroaded are the people of the maritimes. We cannot have energy security at a fair price in Atlantic Canada as long as this Liberal promise remains a Liberal promise. Energy security can only become a reality for us when our own Canadian natural gas is flowing by pipeline to Nova Scotia. We need action, not promises, though it seems, looking back over the years, that we have had more promises than action.
For example, in 1974, 1975 and 1976 the government under the present Prime Minister promised to develop Canadian resources and tar sands and to promote conservation. The minister of energy at that time, Mr. Alastair Gillespie, who had been in favour of self-sufficiency in oil, was compelled to back off by the cabinet of the day in favour of a meaningless policy of "self-reliance". Obviously he was not happy, for in May, 1977, he said it was "-in Canada's interest that we should move our oil price up because any other policy would have disastrous consequences for Canadians in the future." However, despite this far-sighted prediction, the government failed to back Mr. Gillespie.
The thought occurred to me that the Minister of Finance may need these extensive borrowing powers in order to bring about some improvement in regional disparity. This has been a very promising area for the Liberals, for the Prime Minister and his followers. Campaigning in 1980, he promised to build greater economic strength in Canada's regions. In 1968, according to the record, the Prime Minister promised to end regional disparity, and 1 think, without reading every one of his promises, he promised to do this in the course of every election which followed.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that the hour approaches ten o'clock. In closing, I should like to say it ought not to be necessary to remind the government that promises are the paper money of principle and, like our currency, Liberal promises have been greatly devalued over 12 years of reissue. I say it is time to end

May 29, 1980
Adjournment Debate
this charade. It is time to get down to the serious business of governing Canada. We need a new budget and we need one soon. In the absence of a new budget we do not know the facts about the state of our economy, we do not know the facts about the oil price agreement which the government is seeking or the effect rapid increases in oil prices will have on new cash requirements which have to be met.
The Canadian people do not realize the debt burden the government is placing not only on this generation but on generations yet unborn. This is indeed strange conduct for a government under a leader who has promised greater participation by Parliament in solving the nation's problems, a man who promised to bring about the "just society" and who, in 1980, promised to enhance individual security. How can anyone claim to be enhancing the security of individual Canadians while blatantly denying members of this House and, thereby, the Canadian people the facts about the state of the economy?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-SAFETY OF PERSONS LIVING IN PROXIMITY OF PENITENTIARIES
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-SAFETY OF PERSONS LIVING IN PROXIMITY OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of my remarks tonight is to bring to the attention of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) the continuing inadequacy of security measures in our penal institutions with the consequent danger to the residents in the areas where these institutions are located.
Perhaps the residents of my constituency are more sensitive to the dangers than those in other areas because of the fact that we have five federal institutions in the riding, plus two more on the border, and several provincial institutions as well. There are continuing reports of escapes from several of these prisons and the rather lengthy list of incidents has had and is having a very disturbing effect upon the local population.
One of the most recent incidents, the one providing the basis of the present problem, was the escape of an inmate from Mountain prison at Agassiz, British Columbia, and the murder of a local postmaster, and this individual has now been charged with the crime. A protest rally attended by approximately 400 people was held in Agassiz where the local residents, including mayors, community leaders, school representatives and others, expressed their views and called for action to halt this kind of activity.
Numerous communications have been forwarded to the Solicitor General and others, including myself as the member of Parliament for Fraser Valley East, protesting the lack of adequate protection for residents of the community. A school has been closed because of the absence of protective measures to ensure the safety of the staff and pupils.
I should like to read a communication which I received from M. D. Dunn, the mayor of the district of Kent. It refers to communications which he had with the Solicitor General on various occasions. It reads as follows:
Security at Mountain institution has been a major concern of council and the community for many years. By the repeated lack of action to upgrade the security your office must assume the responsibility of the event of April 28, 1980.
This is when the murder took place. It continues:
I feel that past events show that the facilities at this institution arc totally inadequate for a medium security institution and would urge that these prisoners be relocated to other more suitable institutions immediately.
Also I have a telegram from Mayor John Allen of the village of Harrison Hot Springs, and communications from residents, the school board and school principal, all calling for action to deal with this serious danger to private citizens.
The Solicitor General visited the area shortly after this tragic event and I understand he made some commitments. Unfortunately I did not receive an invitation to attend, so I am just taking my information from the reports of it that I received. Certain commitments were made. One was to tighten up security. The second was the construction of a second fence. The third was double gatehouses. The fourth was more adequate perimeter lighting. The fifth was an impact study with local input before any increase in prison population is considered.
May I say that there is a deeping conviction that the two institutions in Kent district, the Kent maximum security institution and Mountain prison, which is a medium security institution, are too great a burden and danger for this area to bear. In discussions with some of the elected officials, I was made aware that Mountain prison should be closed and necessary facilities to house the prison population should be located in some alternate community.
There are a number of problems that have arisen which have caused great concern. One is that apparently there has been a reclassification of prisoners and certain individuals who were previously in the New Westminster penitentiary, which is now closed, were reclassified in order to put them in a lesser security prison because maximum security facilities were not available. When there are one or two individuals who are unruly and are not observant of the rules and regulations of the prison, then trouble can be expected. That is exactly what has happened, and it is causing a great deal of concern among the general prison population.
There have also been escapes from custody when inmates were appearing before provincial court in other parts of the constituency. I have an article here which details the escape of
May 29, 1980

two inmates from the maximum security institution at Kent while appearing in court in Chilliwack. Of course, they were later charged and their sentences extended. Employees of the hospital in my constituency are refusing to provide medical care to prisoners because on a number of occasions they have been faced with incidents in which inmates have drawn knives or guns in an attempt to escape.
I am not blaming the local directors of these institutions. I am saying that the department of the Solicitor General and the minister who propounds the philosophy and implements policies which fail to protect society from those who break the law and endanger the lives of law-abiding citizens, are the guilty ones. I believe that they must be called upon to give reasons why these incidents are happening and why there is such a failure on the part of the authorities to maintain the security of the population in these areas.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Celine Hervieux-Payette (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-SAFETY OF PERSONS LIVING IN PROXIMITY OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to answer the question raised by my colleague, the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Patterson) as I went to the Mountain prison a few days after the incident, and the minister also went through that area on May 10 to assess the situation and discuss with local authorities. So I am pleased to tell him the steps that have been taken during those meetings the minister had and after my report to the minister on my visit before that.
First of all, security measures including a high security double fence, a new perimeter lighting system, new security towers, a new gatehouse, all those additions amounting expenditures of some $ 1.2 million were immediately agreed to by the minister. The officers of the municipalities will be consulted on the plans before they are finalized. There was previous consultation and there will be consultation during the implementation of these new security measures.
In addition, the Solicitor General being aware of the conditions of the roads in the surroundings of the prisons in that area said he is also prepared to consider federal financial contributions toward the improvement of the roads. A study on the community impact will be undertaken by independent consultants before expansion work is undertaken. So, the whole situation, Mr. Speaker, will be reviewed.
Also, a system of notification including a system of audible alarm that could be heard by the residents in the area will be installed so the community will be immediately alerted if other escapes were to take place. Indeed, I would point out to my colleague, who said so previously, that there have been escapes from maximum security penitentiaries, so escapes from a medium security institution are a more likely thing.
In any case, I think those measures will contribute to tighten up security at the institution and will hopefully remedy the problems in my colleague's community.
Adjournment Debate

AIR CANADA-REQUEST RETIREMENT AGE OF PILOTS BE EXTENDED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to share with you on this occasion a matter of deep and troubling concern that Canadians are and will be experiencing at least once in their lifetime. This concern grows out of a question I posed in this House to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) on May 23 regarding the forced retirement of Air Canada pilots at age 60.
During the last two decades we have witnessed the development and establishment of various rights for cultural minorities, rights for men and women, rights for the handicapped, and even rights for gays, to name but a few. It is on this note of human rights that I ask you to focus your attention on the rights of men and women who are forced into retirement by mandatory, bureaucratic policies. As the member for Parkdale-High Park, some of my constituents are turning to me for assistance on this issue, stating that these mandatory retirement policies are not only discriminatory and unjust but are robbing them of meaningful employment and activity.
I bring to your attention, for example, the case of one of my constituents who is a 59-year old Air Canada pilot. He will be forced out of a job soon, simply because he will turn 60 years of age. This constituent, a healthy and alert individual says, simply, "I have worked almost all my life. It has been a real joy and pleasure." In his case this is grossly unjust, especially when one considers that other airlines are permitting their pilots to fly until age 65.
Another constituent of mine who works with the RCMP at Toronto International Airport is being forced to retire this year at age 55. He started working for the RCMP late in life and so, after eight years of work for the RCMP cannot retire with a very large pension. He will have difficulty finding new employment.
These are just two cases from thousands of our Canadian workers who, whether they like it or not, are being put on the shelf. Some have argued and some will argue, that persons should retire because individuals are more prone to heart attacks, strokes and other illnesses after age 60. However, as is pointed out in the report of the Special Senate Committee on Retirement Age Policy entitled "Retirement without Tears", under the chairmanship of Senator David Croll, a gentleman for whom I hold a very high regard:
Compulsory retirement at age 65 could not be justified on medical grounds as a general rule, and for those who did not have enough income, such a compulsory system could sentence them to a life of poverty in their old age-
This has become a real danger, especially during these unstable economic times where inflation threatens pensioners.
One of the government's biggest worries for the future is that a smaller and smaller working population will have to support a larger and larger retired group. As the postwar baby boom generation reaches old age, the figures will zoom, reaching between six and eight million by the year 2031. This

May 29, 1980
Adjournment Debate
problem situation will only be compounded if we continue to permit these mandatory retirement policies to be enforced. To alleviate this most undesirable situation, Mr. Speaker, I propose that this government dedicate itself to implementing the following provisions, outlined by Senator David Croll and his committee.
First, there should be amendments to the rules governing public servants and employees of companies under federal jurisdiction, as well as provincial and municipal public servants.
Second, there should be an increase in the mandatory age of retirement of one year at a time for five years, by amending pension plans or retirement rules and conventions. At the end of five years, the concept of compulsory retirement at a particular age would be dropped.
Third, there should be a review of all human rights legislation to eliminate loopholes which permit age discrimination because of employee benefits and similar plans.
Fourth, there should be created a policy of flexible retirement as the standard for both public and private enterprises.
Mr. Speaker, it is only through the elimination of these and similar discriminatory policies that Canadians will be able to make claim to their "just society". After all, if an individual wants to and is able to work, giving himself a worth-while place in society, then this government should do all in its power to preserve the healthy self-image that many receive from being actively involved in the work force of this great and mighty nation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerald Laniel (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AIR CANADA-REQUEST RETIREMENT AGE OF PILOTS BE EXTENDED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to replace the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bockstael), and attempt to answer the question of the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis).
[ English]
Transport Canada, contrary to the hon. member's pretension, has no retirement age for pilots. The only age requirements is that the applicant must be not less than 21 years of age at the time the licence is issued. This licence must be an airline transport pilot licence, which is a licence required to captain the type of aircraft presently in use by all major airlines' aircraft over 44,000 pounds gross allowable weight for takeoff.
Once the pilot has been issued the licence he can continue to hold it and exercise the privilege of the licence provided that he can continue to meet the medical standards based on those set by ICAO, and pass periodic flight testing to demonstrate his competency. Such testing is done by both the airline company and Transport Canada at least once a year.
At one time the International Civil Aviation Organization on which the Canadian standards are based specified that
pilots who had reached the age of 60 should not be permitted to engage in scheduled or unscheduled international flights. Canada filed a difference with the ICAO and did not adopt this standard since it was considered impracticable and unreasonable.
The latest proposed revision to the international standards, circulated for comment to different organizations, no longer includes such a requirement. Medical and licensing standards are continually under review by Transport Canada and ICAO. The matter of age is always the subject of consideration.
Air Canada, like any other airline or employer, for that matter, sets its own conditions of employment which, of course, include the retirement age for its pilots. Transport Canada has no jurisdiction in such matters. It was impossible therefore for the minister to answer to the satisfaction of the hon. member.
Our responsibility is to ensure that crews are properly licensed and meet the required Transport Canada standards based on those set down by the International Civil Aviation Organization.
The hon. member referred to the special report of the Standing Committee of the Senate entitled "Retirement without Tears."
[ Translation]
Retirement without tears. Well, it may be that he will find the answer to his question in that report and that, eventually, provincial laws and service acts can meet his request but, for the time being, nothing can be done in the Department of Transport.

Mr. Speaker, I rise this late evening hour on a question that I posed to the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe) on April 21, that same fateful evening when a mini-budget or financial statement was introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). At that time I asked the Minister of State for Small Businesses whether or not he cared about small businesses in Canada, whether or not he had specific plans for the small business community, whether he was planning to take action, and if so, what specific action he was planning to launch.
To date we have heard a number of reports in committees about the small business community and some of its concerns, and the programs being proposed have been examined. I can say with a great deal of regret and some hesitation that what I recognize so far are simply extensions of the past. These programs that are being brought forward are nothing more than programs which have been in existence for many, many years. There have been some minor alterations of what can only be considered as totally and completely inadequate. The minister is not addressing the problems of the future, the problems that face Canadian small businesses today and what
May 29, 1980

they will be facing in the years to come. At best one can say that the minister is addressing the problems of small businesses that have existed for the last few decades.
The minister will be the first to say there is legislation now that is of assistance to small businessmen such as the Small Businesses Loans Act. 1 would like to propose that that legislation is completely inadequate. I want to use an example of some persons here in our capital city of Ottawa who put their heads together. They had a fine proposal, a proposal with sound projections and sound cash flows. Four local entrepreneurs were prepared to invest their savings. They were prepared to work toward seeing their dream of a small business established in our capital city. Elowever, to do that they needed $30,000 above their own savings. They were able to pull together $12,000 on their own. They required yet another $30,000, for most enterprises certainly a very small amount of money. They were prepared to put up for collateral, in order to go to the bank, two homes, each worth in excess of $45,000. One individual had silver bars worth at that time $15,000. Together the collateral they were prepared to put forward in order to achieve a $30,000 loan amounted to $105,000, plus a considerable amount of their own money.
First they approached two small branches of the chartered banks. They were rejected outright. They reminded the bankers that there was this Small Businesses Loans Act under which they should be able to purchase the $30,000 loan at prime plus 1 per cent. However, the banker felt they did not have enough collateral.
They then went to two of the downtown main bank branches in this capital city, again interested in applying for a small business loan under the act that should guarantee them a loan at prime plus 1 per cent. The banks said they were not particularly interested in small business at these main branches. They were not particularly interested in encouraging and supporting the small business sector of the community. Furthermore, they said they had some concern that the government was not necessarily a good guarantor and that their experience in the past indicated that the government could not necessarily be relied upon to back up these guarantees.
They had no success with our Canadian chartered banks to arrive at a $30,000 loan with a considerable amount of collateral. Then off they went to the Federal Business Development Bank. 1 am pleased to say that after a considerable amount of time, energy, certainly a great deal of concern, that at this place of last resort for lenders in Canada they were able to achieve a loan. The loan was at an interest rate of 18 per cent and fixed for at least a five-year period.
This is not a typical situation, but in fact the kind of story that small entrepreneurs across our country are continually bringing to Parliament. They remind us of the difficulties they have going into a bank expecting to have access to the small business loans guaranteed by the federal government. There is no risk to the bank, but the one problem, of course, is that it is
Adjournment Debate
only the prime rate plus 1 per cent and the bankers do not know about this act-which has been in existence now, I believe, for 19 years-and are hesitant to bring forward that money.
1 suggest then, as a result of this experience, that the small business entrepreneur in Canada has an unbelievable challenge, and 1 think it was a fair question which 1 asked, whether the Government of Canada really cares about the small businessman in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerald Laniel (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his remarks related to his question asked on April 21.1 will try to answer it to the best of my knowledge. It might not be to his satisfaction, but at least he will have had the opportunity to make his point to the House and to other colleagues.
[Translationj
Mr. Speaker, in the last few months some sectors of society, including small businesses, have shown a lot of concern over rising interest rates. 1 think that the hon. member's question reflected this difficulty. The government recognizes that these high interest rates are a heavy burden for the citizens and businesses of Canada, but the country is also faced with serious inflation problems and controlling them is one of the government's main objective. The current level of interest rates could seriously jeopardize small businesses, but so can inflation.
1 am not an economist but I know that interest rates help control inflation and maintain the value of the dollar. This may be a simplification but it is widely recognized. In the Speech from the Throne, on April 14 last, the government committed itself to help those Canadians most affected by rising interest rates including small businessmen. Two bills have already passed second reading and have been referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. Bill C-17, to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, raises the maximum loan from $75,000 to $100,000 and provides for loans totalling $850 million which will be granted over the next two years. Also, Bill C-20 makes it possible for the Federal Development Bank to offer more financial aid to small businesses. Or again, in the more general sector, through the Income Tax Act, the government provides new fiscal measures concerning bonds for the development of small businesses and the transfer of deductions between spouses. Finally, for a longer term, the Economic Council of Canada is currently studying matters concerning small business and another study has been undertaken jointly by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Canadian Banks Association.
Since his appointment, the Minister of State for Small Businesses has consulted with all the important associations of small businesses in Canada and he has met with a large

May 29, 1980
Adjournment Debate
number of independent businessmen. It has not taken him a very long time to understand that the small business would in fact encounter difficulties in the period we are currently going through.

In short, Mr. Speaker, this government is addressing economic issues faced by this country, head on. It is committed to fighting inflation and it is committed to the Canadian small business community. It is committed to the short-term and the long-term solution.
I can assure the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) that not all small businesses are going bankrupt. Very
few, less than 1 per cent, are going bankrupt, which is a standard and recognized historical figure.
We remain very positive with respect to the opportunities which small businesses will be faced with in the months to come. We are also positive toward the government's commitment to the Canadian small business community.
